subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  APPOINTMENT OF TEMPORARY CONSULTANTS IN FINANCE DEPARTMENT

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  APPOINTMENT OF TEMPORARY CONSULTANTS IN FINANCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege that has to do with the relations between the executive and parliament and therefore is of concern to all members of this house.
On Friday last the Minister of Finance informed the house that certain gentlemen had been appointed on a temporary basis to the Department of Finance. The minister gave the number and date of the treasury board minute which was supposed to have effected these appointments.
Yesterday I asked the Minister of Finance if this treasury board minute, and another one, had been validated by order in council. He expressed the opinion that this had been done, but said he would look into it. My searches have revealed no such order in council. I was in communication again today, as is my right, with the privy council office, and I was informed then that there still are no orders in council supporting either of the treasury board minutes to which reference has now been made by the Minister of Finance.
My point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is twofold. On the one hand, we were misled by the Minister of Finance when we were told that these gentlemen were appointed to the Department of Finance, because their appointments are completely irregular. On the other hand, we have a point of privilege in that a section of the Financial Administration Act has been violated. I refer, as I did yesterday, to section 5, subsection 2, of the Financial Administration Act which reads as follows:
The governor in council may authorize the treasury board to exercise all or any of the powers other than powers of appointment-
May I repeat those words, which are very clear:
-other than powers of appointment, of the governor in council under the Civil Service Act, the Civil Service Superannuation Act, the Defence Services Pension Act, and parts II to VI of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act.
It is very clear, Mr. Speaker, that one power the treasury board does not have, a power that cannot be given to it even by the governor in council, is the power of appointment; yet by treasury board minutes T.B. 610618 dated May 2, 1963 and T.B. 610952 dated May 17, 1963, first three and then a fourth person were presumably appointed to the Department of Finance on a temporary basis. In view of the fact that the treasury board had no such authority, and in view of the fact that appointments could only be made by the governor in council, this means that when these four gentlemen were working with the Minister of Finance on the budget they were not properly attached to the Department of Finance because the treasury board had no authority to make any such appointments.
As I have indicated, my point of privilege is twofold. First, we have been misled in being told that these gentlemen were attached, even temporarily, to the Department of Finance. Such was not the case. They were complete outsiders, just as anyone else might be, because their appointments were not regular.
The second aspect of my point of privilege is that just as in the last session the Financial Administration Act was misused-and hon. gentlemen now on the government side complained about its misuse-so it is now again being misused because the clear provisions against the treasury board making appointments have been violated.
If an order in council is now produced trying to make this validation retroactive it will not change the fact that during the time these gentlemen were assisting the Minister of Finance in the preparation of the budget they were complete outsiders.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  APPOINTMENT OF TEMPORARY CONSULTANTS IN FINANCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first place I certainly had no intention of misleading the house, nor do I think I did so. If I did I apologize, but I do not think I did.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked me the other day what authority there was for the appointment of the special consultants in question. In my reply I said the treasury board minutes are submitted to council in the normal course, and I promised to look into the matter and to report what had actually taken place. Now, very little time has elapsed. I looked into the

Question of Privilege
matter this morning, and this is the answer I was going to give to my hon. friend on orders of the day.
The answer is that the special consultants were employed by service contract, approved by the treasury board, pursuant to the government contracts regulations. These government contracts regulations were themselves established by the governor in council under the authority of section 39 of the Financial Administration Act.
The government contracts regulations require that service contracts in excess of $1,000 be approved by the treasury board. I am informed by the secretary of the treasury board and by the solicitor in the Department of Finance that section 5(2) of the Financial Administration Act, to which my hon. friend referred, does not apply in these cases, and that no other authority was required other than the treasury board minutes referred to previously. I am informed that this is the practice that has been followed by successive governments for many years.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance which arises out of a statement in an article in the Toronto Globe and Mail of Friday, June 14, to the effect that oil and gas pipe line companies will be allowed to deduct from income expenses incurred in drilling for

oil and gas. This proposal would be backdated to April 10, 1962, according to the newspaper statement. Is this true?

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: OIL AND GAS
subsubtopic: DEDUCTION OF DRILLING AND EXPLORATION EXPENSES
speechtext:
This provision, Mr. Speaker, is set out in paragraph 4 of the income tax regulations on pipe line companies and exploration extensions. The proposal that companies whose principal business is operating a pipe line be allowed to deduct drilling and exploration expenses is a logical extension or rounding out of provisions in the Income Tax Act concerning the deduction of exploration expenses. Some of these existing provisions of the act have been there for many years; others were added only last year.
In 1947 provisions providing tax credits on account of exploration and drilling expenses were changed to the present method of allowing these expenses as a deduction from income. Since that time this right of oil and gas companies to deduct exploration and drilling expenses has been gradually broadened.
In March, 1957 a change was announced, effective for 1957 and subsequent years, which permitted companies whose principal business is processing mineral ores for the purpose of recovering metals therefrom, or processing metals from the ores so processed, to deduct all expenses incurred in searching for minerals in Canada or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas in Canada. The purpose of this amendment was to permit companies engaged in processing ores into metals, such as steel companies, to deduct the cost of exploring for supplies of the raw materials used in their business.
In June, 1961 the budget speech announced an extension of this provision to include companies whose principal business is fabricating metals. This permitted companies that take prime metal, such as copper, and manufacture or process it into finished goods to deduct the expenses of exploring for minerals or oil or gas in Canada.
In April, 1962 the budget speech announced further concessions for the oil and gas industry and for those interested in exploring for oil, gas or minerals. These concessions included a provision which permitted any individual or company to deduct expenses incurred in drilling or exploring for oil or gas in Canada from the income of that person from the operation of an oil or gas well in Canada. These concessions were made available to all individuals whether or not they were residents of Canada, and to all
Inquiries of the Ministry companies irrespective of any degree of Canadian ownership or control. These 1962 concessions probably benefited foreign owned and controlled companies to a much greater extent than Canadians.
In May, 1963 representatives of six pipe line companies made representations to the government urging that pipe line companies be allowed to deduct from income the expenses they incurred in drilling and exploring for oil and gas reserves in Canada. At this meeting I was represented by Mr. Benson, parliamentary secretary to the Department of Finance, and a permanent official of the department.
These companies already were permitted under the 1962 legislation to deduct exploration and drilling expenses from any income they had from the operation of an oil or gas well in Canada, or from royalties in respect of an oil or gas well, but they pointed out that they had very little such income. They also pointed out that the existing law denied the same right of deduction as oil and gas companies only because of a technical interpretation of the law which held that transportation of oil or gas did not qualify as marketing of these products.
It was pointed out on behalf of these companies that they are virtually dependant upon a supply of oil and gas to keep them in business, and it was represented that they had as good a reason to be allowed to deduct the cost of hunting for the raw materials upon which their business is based as companies engaged in fabricating metals.
These representations appeared to the government to be reasonable and worthy of favourable action. Most important of all was the fact that the majority of the companies to benefit from this further concession would be Canadian residents, and have a high degree of Canadian ownership.
The representations made in writing by the pipe line companies did not ask that any legislation be retroactive, and so far as those who represented the government at the meeting can recall this matter was not discussed. It was the general understanding that the companies were looking forward to the deduction of expenses they planned to make in the future and that they had no expenses incurred in the past which they hoped to be able to deduct. The decision to have the proposed amendment date from April 10, 1962 was made following a recommendation made entirely on technical grounds by those engaged in drafting the resolution.
Because of the nature of the extensive amendments made in 1962 to section 838A of the Income Tax Act to implement the 1962

Inquiries of the Ministry budget proposals related to the oil and gas industry, it was necessary to divide exploration and drilling expenses into those incurred before April 10, 1962 and those incurred after that date. The division is made in subsections 3, 3b, 3c, 3d, 4a, 4b, 4c, 5a, 5b, 5c, and 6a of section 83A. It was believed that to add a new date from which exploration and drilling expenses would be measured would seriously complicate an already complex section of the Income Tax Act. For this reason, and for this reason only, paragraph 4 of the income tax resolution proposes that the change related to pipe line companies date from April 10, 1962.

In reply to the hon. member may I say at the outset, especially with regard to this final point, that the Journals reflect what took place in the house yesterday. However, I realize the general interest in this matter and I should like to make a short statement which I hope will be of interest and of use to the house.
It has come to my attention, especially through the hon. member who has just spoken, that some doubt has arisen with respect to the terms of the question upon which the house divided yesterday. Obviously we cannot turn back and alter any proceedings that took place yesterday, nor should any discussion in relation thereto be permitted at this time. However, as mentioned in paragraph 4, citation 70 of Beauchesne's fourth edition:
A point of order against procedure must be raised before the question has passed to a stage at which the objection would be out of place.
And further on, standing order 35 states:
No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
However, by consent of the house I could say a few words in an effort to dissolve any confusion with regard to yesterday's proceedings which may now exist in the minds of some hon. members; that is, if the house so desires.
Yesterday, as hon. members will recall, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition asked leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 and stated the matter which he proposed for discussion.
A discussion then arose with regard to the urgency of the matter to be discussed. After contributions from several hon. members the Chair decided, in effect, that, as the matter could be discussed and voted upon in the course of the budget debate which would begin Wednesday next, the proposal was not a matter of urgency of debate under the terms of standing order 26 as understood and accepted by the practice of this house.
Inquiries of the Ministry
At this point in the proceedings the following is recorded at page 1240 of yesterday's Hansard:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF VOTE ON JUNE 17
speechtext: I must regretfully appeal from your ruling.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF VOTE ON JUNE 17
speechtext:
Before the ruling is appealed, may I make one further short comment? My predecessors have many times in the past expressed the view that there is no appeal of a decision taken by the Speaker under standing order 26.
In this regard, I refer hon. members to a ruling made by my immediate predecessor on January 31, 1963, which appears at page 3297 of Hansard. Therefore, I am making a similar ruling.
It is at this stage in the proceedings that the difficulty arises.
It was my opinion that I had given a second ruling, namely, that there was no appeal of a decision taken by the Speaker under standing order 26. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as recorded at page 1240 of Hansard, then used the following words:
That ruling to which you have just referred, Mr. Speaker, was reversed by a vote of the house, and I submit that a decision of the house stands over the decision which was made by Mr. Speaker Lambert.
Since it is a well established rule that no debate is permitted on any ruling, the Chair interpreted the interposition of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as an appeal to the house from the second ruling.
It would appear to me that, in effect, the house yesterday was confirming a ruling that there could be no appeal of a decision taken by Mr. Speaker under standing order 26 and that such a decision of the house would be valid for the duration of the current session. However, in putting the question to the house the Chair stated that the appeal was from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and thereby hangs our difficulty.
Some hon. members may feel that they might have voted otherwise had the question been stated in other terms and, in reviewing the records, there may be justification for the taking of that position. Notwithstanding the fact that it is not open to the Chair or to any other member to review, alter or even to interpret any prior proceedings, I would like however to proffer a suggestion for the consideration of the house at this time. Since the question, as put from the Chair, may have been interpreted differently, it is my suggestion that yesterday's vote be considered as not being binding should a similar situation arise later in this session.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, June 17, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Pickersgill-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Atlantic Development Board Act to increase the number of members of the Atlantic development board from five to eleven; to establish as a separate account in the consolidated revenue fund an Atlantic development fund to which shall be credited the sum of one hundred million dollars to be used for the purpose of financing or assisting in financing programs or projects that would contribute to the growth and development of the economy of the Atlantic region and for which satisfactory financing arrangements are not otherwise available; and to provide that the said act shall expire on the 24th day of January, 1969; and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the said act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Order. House again in committee of the whole on a certain proposed resolution to amend the Atlantic Development Board Act. Shall the resolution carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the resolution now before the committee is one in which we who are here representing various communities in the Atlantic provinces have a great deal of interest. It was my understanding-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I am finding it difficult to hear the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. I wonder if we might have order in the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Order. Perhaps hon. members would hasten their departures from the chamber and those remaining would observe silence so that we can hear the hon. member.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, all could hear if the Secretary of State would only exercise a little more discipline over on his side. I was observing that this was a resolution in which we from the Atlantic provinces have a tremendous amount of interest. Prior to the speech of the Secretary of State yesterday I was under the impression that some phases of it, for instance the increases in membership of the board, were contemplated for the purpose of securing representation for groups of people who, in the opinion of the government, might not be represented. However, since his speech yesterday I find that it is contemplated that the present membership are not to be continued in office for any great length of time. The members of the board are going to be continued in office for the period of one year. The chairman presumably will be demoted to member, and he is going to be continued for two years; and that will be the end of his actions and function as a member of the board.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent the situation. The situation is that their present terms, if the house accepts the bill, will be continued by legislation for that period, and they will be eligible for reappointment in all cases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: What a chance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is quite clear, I think.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is my opinion that we are going to find that this is a gimmick to get rid of the present members of the board.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is exactly what it is.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I think in that connection it might be well if we examined the present personnel of the board.

As was pointed out yesterday, very properly, by my hon. friend from Royal this board has been set up. This board is prepared to function. This board has a full membership. This board has a membership representing every province of the Atlantic provinces. This board is composed of men who are outstanding and who were selected for that particular reason and not for any narrow, partisan consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Hon.
members may laugh but they do not understand that language. Our friends opposite, Mr. Chairman, do not understand it, especially those from the Atlantic provinces. We have on the board an outstanding executive director from the civil service of Canada, a most outstanding man. The selection of official personnel for this board, which was not large, was an attempt to get a representative from each province, and as my hon. friend the Secretary of State knows, that was done. I am sure he will be the first to agree that the officials of the board are very capable people. I submit that the members of the board are also outstanding in every respect. There is no need for any resolution to come before this committee to introduce a measure to amend the Atlantic Development Board Act, because the Atlantic Development Board Act does not need any amending. The Atlantic Development Board Act should be continued in the form passed by the previous government last December. It should be allowed to function.
In the course of some remarks, a few weeks ago I made this observation: why does not the government allow the Atlantic development board to function for at least a year, and then if the government find there is something which might be improved they could bring forward legislation and ask for an amendment, but, Mr. Chairman, the government are asking us to amend something which has not even started, which I submit is a ridiculous situation.
Coming back to the personnel of the board, we have as its vice chairman Mr. Frank Sobey, of Nova Scotia, one of the most outstanding industrialists not only in Nova Scotia but all Canada. I might call the attention of the committee to an article written in the Montreal Gazette of May 24, which was only a few days ago, by Mr. John Meyer, the financial editor, in which he compares the Industrial Estates, of which Mr. Sobey is president, with the proposed set-up for the Quebec government. Then Mr. Meyer goes on to say:
Industrial Estates, in the six years since it was set up by the Nova Scotia government, has assisted
18, 1963
Atlantic Development Board Act in the establishment of 31 new industrial plants in the province. Seven of these have been established since the beginning of the year. They include Volvo, the Swedish automobile manufacturer, J. F. Cross-ley, the British carpet manufacturer, and, the most recent, the aluminum can plant for Reynolds International. Negotiations are in process with a number of other companies-
-for more industrial establishments. Those last four words are mine. Now, Mr. Chairman, this is the gentleman who, according to this legislation, is going to have notice served on him that his services are required only for a period of a year and then he is through. That is what is contemplated by the resolution, as explained by the Secretary of State yesterday.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I have already contradicted that once. Does the hon. gentleman not accept my word that Mr. Sobey will be eligible for reappointment for another three-year term?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Eligible. The people of Nova Scotia will love to hear that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I will
tell you what will change my attitude towards this resolution. If the Secretary of State wants to get up and say that Mr. Sobey will be continued for his full term, all right. I am surprised that members on the Liberal side from any part of the Atlantic provinces would ever subscribe to this type of resolution. If it went through the caucus of members on the government side representing the Atlantic provinces, then I am very much surprised. I am quite surprised that the Secretary of State would sponsor it. After all, he does represent an Atlantic province. He has adopted one of the Atlantic provinces. Therefore I am surprised that he should bring this resolution forward because it contemplates that six new members will be appointed to the board. At present there are five.
I have referred to Mr. Sobey, the outstanding contribution he has made and the high respect in which he is held in the Atlantic provinces. No one will dispute that, I am sure. The government apparently has decided that it does not want his services for any length of time. With that I do not agree.
Let us go to some of the others. When I occupied a position of some responsibility in connection with this matter not once did I hear any criticism of Mr. McQuaid of Prince Edward Island, the former attorney general. Oh, some of my hon. friends may say that he is a defeated cabinet minister. In my book that is a compliment so far as his performing service is concerned, and if he was unsuccessful in one election I am sure there are many of us who will understand that that is no particular disgrace. It is simply a trend of political fortune. But never once did I hear

Atlantic Development Board Act from anyone any objection to him from the point of view of his ability. Quite the opposite was the case. Every comment in connection with Mr. McQuaid's appointment was complimentary, and I might say that even in such a happy family as the Conservatives comments are not always complimentary. There never was any objection to Mr. McQuaid.
The same thing applies to Mr. Fred Ayre, the representative from Newfoundland. I have heard no adverse criticism of his appointment from my friends from the province of Newfoundland who sit in this House of Commons. He is an outstanding man in every respect. The gentleman who represents New Brunswick, Mr. Lalande, enjoys a tremendously good reputation in that province. The only criticism I have heard of him is that he comes from the province of Quebec. That is the only adverse criticism, if it is a criticism, I have ever heard in connection with Mr. Lalande. He is a banker. He is a supervisor for the Provincial Bank of Canada located at Moncton and he enjoys a most excellent reputation.
These are the gentlemen who are affected by the resolution which says that we should amend the Atlantic Development Board Act by increasing the number of members from five to eleven. I have said that I consider this to be a gimmick by which the government is going to put an end to the services of the people now occupying these positions. The Secretary of State takes issue with that statement. He says they are eligible but he does not say they will be reappointed. He does not say they will be continued in office. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, if the government wanted to do what is best for the Atlantic provinces and for Canada they would let the membership of the board continue as it is for a certain length of time anyway, because they cannot get better men. I am one of those who do not say that one man is better than another. I say you would not get better men than those who have been selected.
The publisher of the Fredericton Gleaner and the Atlantic Advocate is a personal friend of mine. There is no question about that. I have great personal regard for Brigadier Wardell. Over the last 11 or 12 years he has adopted the Atlantic provinces. He has proclaimed the gospel of the Atlantic provinces from one end of Canada to the other. He has carried the torch. If you will refer to previous copies of the Atlantic Advocate you will find that he suggests that his interest is entirely unselfish and objective and that he is simply anxious to make a contribution to our part of Canada. I do not believe anyone will take exception to that proposition. I think we in the Atlantic

provinces are anxious to have influential people from all over the world come and take an interest in our part of Canada. I am sure that is the feeling of most of us. This is what we have in the person of Brigadier Wardell.
Those are the members of the board that this legislation is designed, I say, to get rid of. I do not think there is any need for this resolution. All that the government needed to do was to continue the board in office and allow it to function as it was intended to under the direction of a minister, of course. So far as the selection of a minister is concerned I find no fault with the selection of the Secretary of State. As a matter of fact, I was quite happy when that selection was made because I felt that he would bring to the four provinces a somewhat detached interest of any one province compared with another. I hope I am right about that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: The height of optimism.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps it is the height of optimism. A question was asked in the house before as to the disposition of the money. I will come to that in a few minutes. So far as the official duties of the Secretary of State are concerned, I suggest to him that he extend his horizon beyond the narrow partisanship of the Liberal party. I would ask him to look towards development and progress in the Atlantic provinces and accept his new responsibility as an instrument by which he can render a tremendous service to those provinces and the region which has adopted him. He has been re-elected time and time again and I find no particular fault with that. That is the right of the people of every community. But I do think it brings with it a degree of responsibility not only to his constituents but also to the region which in this case the minister represents. Therefore I ask him to use his position not in a narrow and partisan way but for the general good of that part of Canada. May I say that I think he is probably somewhat less partisan than some of his colleagues.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Some
members may laugh but I still think that is the case. I refer now to the board, its personnel and the first few words of the resolution which say that "it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Atlantic Development Board Act". I am opposed to this. I do not think it should be amended. I think the board should be continued as is. Even if the members of the board to whom I have just referred continued in office any length of

time they would be outvoted for sure and it is my opinion that they would be voted out.
I have said that the board is just getting started and there is no record to discuss. There are no actions to examine. There are no results to analyse. However, there has been a change in government and someone has decided to make a change in the board. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that that is not in the best interests of the Atlantic provinces, nor is it in the best interests of Canada as a whole.
Now, perhaps they think that this is a politically expedient thing to do. I submit they are wrong if they think it is politically expedient. It is not the politically expedient thing to do. The political expedient thing to do is to have this board function in order that it can perform the services for which it was established and clothed with the legislative authority by the previous parliament. The board should be allowed to examine things.
May I, at the risk of being repetitious repeat what I said in this house a few months ago when the board was set up? These remarks applied then and they apply now. I am quoting now:
So I point out, Mr. Chairman, the need of addressing ourselves to the problem of creating job opportunities in our own region-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Can the hon. member give the page in Hansard?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
This is not Hansard, it is the Atlantic Advocate and contains a condensation of Hansard. I think the hon. member will agree with me that it is a correct report. I am sure it is, and I am sure he has no reason to believe otherwise. It is much easier to get at, and our research facilities are somewhat limited. If I quote incorrectly I will be the first to acknowledge it.
-and then, looking at the transportation problem and also paying some special attention to the possibilities of cultivating markets where we may have natural advantages compared with other parts of Canada by reason of our location on the Atlantic seaboard.
Anything wrong with that, Mr. Chairman? Is this not what we have been harping about ever since this session started, job opportunities?
The Atlantic development board will inquire into and report to the government suggesting measures with respect to projects which promise to accelerate the growth of the area's economy.
Anything wrong with that, Mr. Chairman?
It will consider and report after investigation on projects suggested by provincial governments and other parties. This is in accordance with the statement of the Prime Minister in April last.
Atlantic Development Board Act
The reason I mention these things, Mr. Chairman, is simply this: That was the concept of the Atlantic development board, and in my opinion that is still the concept in the hearts and minds of the members of this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: What about the money?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend talks about money. He sold the people of his constituency a bill of goods on that proposition. Since he has reminded me of this aspect in the matter, I may say there never was any question about funds being available to this board. During the election campaign our opponents tried to convince the public that there was no money. Well, the whole resources of Canada were behind this board. I have just read from my own remarks, and it is clear that after investigation the board, under the old legislation, made its report to the minister responsible. In this case, it would be the Secretary of State. If the Secretary of State were favourably disposed towards the recommendations, he carried them to his colleagues in the government. I submit, therefore, that the whole of the resources of Canada were behind the board as it was constituted under the legislation.
There was no limit; but there is a limit now unless the minister will tell me that this $100 million fund that has been set up is only a beginning. I submit that there are many situations in the Atlantic provinces deserving of examination and investigation. These investigations could result in the processing of raw materials presently imported into the country. From the point of view of our balance of payments position, therefore, this plan has a good deal of merit. In so far as the $100 million is concerned, I want the minister to say that the $100 million is mentioned purely as an amount to draw against. The time allotted for this board to be in existence under this legislation is six years. After that, it is going to die. We have four provinces, so the unit is 24 and if we divide that into 100 we find that there will be $4 million per year for each province.
I am one of those who believes that the Atlantic provinces, or for that matter any other province, do not want to build up their economy at the expense of the rest of Canada, except in unusual circumstances. These unusual circumstances might be the securing and processing of certain materials which are strategic and which are presently being imported.
Let me come back to the question of the amount of money that will be available to the board. It seems to me that we are rather attaching altogether too much importance to figures. The Secretary of State answered a

Atlantic Development Board Act question yesterday from the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria and said that the $100 million is much better than nothing. It has been suggested that there was no money available. I am suggesting now, in all seriousness, that that is not a proper inference because all the resources of Canada were behind this board. They would be under the present government too, I am convinced, if they would just allow the board to continue.
You recall what happened, Mr. Chairman, in connection with the legislation which was passed by the federal government to assist in the Beechwood development. I have mentioned this before. The previous parliament was only asked to vote the amount necessary to pay for the project, but that is being repaid each year. It makes no difference what government is in office in New Brunswick, the money will be repaid. This was the concept at that time, and still is the concept so far as that is concerned. We needed someone to endorse our note, and it was as simple as that. Then, we were able to borrow the money on a more attractive basis, thus enabling us to deliver electricity at a cheaper price to the public and attract industry into that part of the country.
Let us take the Atlantic provinces power development program, a measure adopted when a good many hon. members were here. They voted for it. I suggest there has been something like $25 million to $30 million spent on transmission lines and in building plants in the Atlantic provinces. The electric power commissions purchase them and have a 30-year period to make payment for plants and a 40-year period in connection with transmission lines, so in the long run it costs the federal government nothing in so far as these two projects are concerned.
I am sure every hon. member from the Atlantic provinces will agree with this. They have contributed tremendously to the economic development of our part of Canada.
The reason I mention these things is simply because this is what we envisaged when the act was passed, and we received support from the then opposition. We appreciated that support at the time, and still do; but why our hon. friends opposite should now do a right about face, and first of all provide that they are going to nullify the work of these able people I have mentioned, then, second, provide that the act go out of existence on January 24, 1969, is surprising. Why they set a date for this act to die is something I cannot understand. That is something they should leave to the next parliament to decide. This parliament should not be legislating categorically for something that is going to come up in 1969. That is basically wrong, particularly


when it affects the lives, activities and the general standards of people in one part of Canada. However, that is what the resolution calls for and I am sure, you, Mr. Chairman, can quite understand my objection to it.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I also wish to thank the Secretary of State. I am sure the things I am saying are so pleasant that he would want me to continue. Surely those of us in this house who represent the Atlantic provinces should be able to agree on objectives. We might disagree on the way to achieve those objectives, but surely the objectives must include the betterment and improvement of all the citizens of the Atlantic provinces who have honoured us in electing us as their representatives?
I wonder if the Liberals have had a caucus on this matter. I wonder if they all voted for this resolution which is going to sound the death knell of the Atlantic development board. Yes, Mr. Chairman, this resolution sets the date when it is going to die.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Gloom and doom.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
They do need to shake their heads. All they need to do is read the resolution. On January 24, 1969 it dies. There is no question about that. Yesterday we had an explanation given to us by the Secretary of State in connection with this matter, but rather than reassuring me it disturbed me. He said that the suggested change would have significance on the effectiveness of the board for the short duration of its lifetime. The short span that is contemplated is six years and the resolution then provides for the death of the board. If the government gives the matter second thought I do not think it will continue with a resolution such as that.
I would also like to ask what are to be the qualifications of the six additional members? Last year hon. members who now sit on the government side were very worried about whether or not some defeated Conservative candidate might be appointed. Well, Mr. Chairman, to me a defeated candidate

is a man of ability. He just has not been able to get enough votes, and that is all. It could be a temporary situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Labour subscribes to that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That will be his position in the next election.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Will these six men to be appointed be employers of labour, manufacturers, industrialists, representatives of organized labour or representatives of the provincial governments?
The chairman of the Atlantic development board has said the members will carry on with their work. I am not going to transgress on the good will of the house by dealing at length with the speech which he made the other day, but in that speech he said he had been in consultation with the Secretary of State and he proposed to carry on. He also said that the job they had to do was greater than any personal attributes of any kind. I submit that is a very fine, broadminded attitude to take.
Before this debate finishes the Secretary of State might tell us whom he proposes to put on this board.

I have one more point to make, and perhaps we may get a chance to have a few words on the bill itself in committee. But at this stage, I would like to speak about the need for those of us who come from the Atlantic provinces to indicate to the rest of Canada that we are no longer going to be subject to the rule of divide and conquer. For years they have taken very outstanding people from the Atlantic provinces and brought them to Ottawa. This applies to both sides of politics, and for years they threw an odd breakwater to us, and an odd wharf to Newfoundland. They made us smile and like it, and that was about all we ever received prior to 1957. But, since 1957 a new dispensation has been ushered into the Atlantic provinces and no longer is the uniform application of an over-all principle considered good enough.
The principle of the Conservative party is that special situations demand special attention and consideration. That is something I hope we could all agree on, and so I am going to make an appeal to those on the opposite side who represent the Atlantic provinces, and especially to the Secretary of State, that they just forget about this whole question of making changes to the act; that they just allow it to stand as it is, and let it succeed or fall on the things that it is able to accomplish for the Atlantic provinces.
But give it a fair chance and do not condemn it immediately by an amendment that would really put it out of business so far as the original board is concerned. Let us go ahead and try it out. If one year hence it is decided that some improvements can be made, well and good; let the minister bring it back to this parliament. But to condemn something that has never yet had a chance to function or perform any service for this part of Canada is, in my opinion, unfair and getting quite close to being absolutely dishonest.

Mr. Chairman, last year I took part in the debate on the legislation concerning the creation of the Atlantic development board, and it is with pleasure that I now find myself, once again, on familiar ground. I have always taken a keen interest in the maritime provinces, partly because of the spiritual bonds which tie us to the maritime provinces, and partly because those provinces carry the burden of an underdeveloped economy.
On the other hand, the people of Saguenay region are closely linked with the Acadians. After one of the first Acadians was deported, his son left Philadelphia and crossed the border to found the colony around lake St. John. His name was Nicolas de Tolentin Hebert. So that we have yet another reason to think of the future of that part of Acadia and of the maritime provinces.
In addition, the people of the province of Quebec recently subscribed $150,000 to save a French newspaper, L'Evangeline, from extinction. I made a contribution and I am glad I did because we wish to maintain French culture in that part of the country.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, when I think that the government is considering an amendment to the legislation we adopted last year to increase from five to eleven the number of members who sit on the board, I wonder if that is not merely to check the action of the five Conservatives-if they are all Conservatives-who were appointed by the previous government. If that were the case, it would be petty politics, and I hope that is not the government's aim when it proposes to increase the number of commissioners from five to eleven.
I do not want to impute motives to anybody but I find this attitude of the government rather odd. Of course, without knowing personally the present members of that board, I do believe they were appointed because of their qualifications and I think they should be able to do their job.
[Mr. Flemming (Victoria-Carleton) .1

However, if the number of commissioners is raised to eleven to allow for a more efficient representation of each of the Atlantic regions, that is of each county in particular and especially those which are the most economically affected, the idea might have some sense.
Last year, we set forth definite ideas on the matter in this house, and I am pleased to call the attention of the house to what our national leader, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) stated, as shown in Hansard. I quote:
(Text):
One word that Social Credit will never use in connection with its policy for the maritimes is the word "welfare". Nor will it refer to the eastern provinces of Canada as a "depressed area". The truth is, and all of Canada should realize it, that the maritime provinces are potentially the richest and the most prosperous in the whole of Canada. The maritimes are not a "depressed", they are an "emerging" area.
If one looks, not at the problems of the Atlantic area, but at its resources, these are amazing. Prince Edward Island is one of the richest farming areas in the dominion. Nova Scotia has big reserves of coal, is excellently placed as a centre for shipping, and for the fishing industry. New Brunswick is not only the centre of a new base metal mining industry, and a major source of timber, but it is the site for some of the leading universities on the North American continent-an asset without price in an age where the "baby boom" coupled with a growing demand for higher education has put a premium on higher learning. Newfoundland and Labrador have immense and undeveloped potentials in hydroelectric power, fishing, lumbering and mining. All this is without mentioning the possibilities of the area for tourism, and the fact that the vast market of New York state is highly accessible by land and sea.
The basic problem of the Atlantic area is not one of resources; it is one of markets. Particularly, it is one of trade to the natural outlet of the area-the eastern United States, hampered by Canada's high tariff policy ever since the end of reciprocity in the years before confederation. Were this barrier removed, iron ore from Labrador would be smelted in Nova Scotia before being shipped to New York-instead of going directly and filling the furnaces of the middle west. Prince Edward Island farm products could break in on the American market-something that might also make undertaking the Chignecto canal worth while.
Power and raw material resources could be developed. In terms of development, the Atlantic provinces could become the British Columbia of the eastern seaboard.
(Translation):
Those are the very sensible words that were spoken here by our national leader, the hon. member for Red Deer, and I am pleased to endorse them at this time.
Now, Mr. Chairman, on reading the resolution, I note that the government intends to establish a $100 million fund in order to foster a real development in the Atlantic area. Of course, this is a most commendable and

realistic purpose, because it is not with next to nothing that the development of the maritime provinces can be promoted, but with capital. But, Mr. Chairman, what good can $100 million do for the development of the Atlantic provinces when one considers their needs? In my opinion, an amount of $100 million is only a drop in the ocean.
In order to develop the maritime provinces, at least $1 billion is needed, that is, at least $100 million every year. Therefore, $100 million are not enough. Provision should be made for that when the bill itself is introduced so that a worth-while program may be established in that regard.
I also noticed that this government is again considering, as it does for other projects, taking this money out of the consolidated revenue fund, which comes from taxation. I wonder how anyone can have such old-fashioned notions in 1963 and how anyone can, from an economic point of view, want to establish anything by taxing individuals again.
We already know that the people in the maritime provinces, as those in other areas of Canada, are overtaxed. It is no use taking money from Joe to give it to Henry. New capital must be created, as we explained during the debate on a measure concerning the municipal development and loan board. We need new capital to satisfy the needs of Canada. We cannot be satisfied with old capital that is capital already existing. We do not have enough capital. Therefore we must create new capital. Now, the Bank of Canada is the only organization capable of creating such capital, because it is the people's bank, the bank of the Canadian people, and consequently the bank of all the people in the maritime provinces. The people in the maritime provinces expect their government, if it really wants to make an effort to be of assistance to them, to participate in a vast maritime development, so that these provinces may have their own industry and keep their population at home.
Therefore, it is absolutely necessary to create new capital, and this new capital will have to be supplied by the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada will have to be entrusted with the responsibility for creating this capital to finance the expenses necessary for the development of the Atlantic provinces.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the few remarks I wanted to make in this debate. I hope that the government will consider them, because if we take the trouble to make suggestions or

I want to begin by reiterating a statement made by my hon. friend the Secretary of State concerning the amount of money which it is envisaged would be expended on the rehabilitation of the economy of the Atlantic provinces. The Secretary of State certainly did not wish to imply, and neither did any other member of this party wish to imply at any time, that the $100 million set forth in the present resolution would be the total sum to be expended for this purpose. As the Secretary of State said, rather repetitiously, I thought, this was merely to be a stopgap fund. Various departments of government were to be especially active in relation to the Atlantic provinces. This particular fund would be supplementary to the increased activity of the ordinary departments of government.
My main purpose in rising is to make a comment on the basic argument put forward this afternoon by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. As I understood it, this argument was: we have before us an act of parliament, an act which was passed in the last parliament, and the present parliament should give that legislation a trial run. That was the plea made by the hon. member. Well, he was here in the last parliament and he knows what took place. He knows that those of us who were then on the other side of the house believed that though the program embodied in the act which is now under consideration moved in the right direction, it did not move far enough or emphatically enough in that direction. We argued that it was not strong enough. We argued that the board should be strengthened. However, in that parliament, our arguments did not prevail.
Then an election took place, and in the course of the campaign leading up to April 8, certain persons now members of this house delivered speeches which were made seriously by them, and taken seriously by many of their constituents. For example, in my own constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough I occasionally made reference to a pamphlet entitled, "A Better Break for the Atlantic Provinces". From that pamphlet I read a paragraph stating that Liberal policies would include "providing a stronger Atlantic development board with a capital assistance fund to promote basic development projects and to encourage the expansion of industry to provide jobs and income".

Atlantic Development Board Act
I am sure the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton can scarcely object to my taking the position in this parliament, which meets here as a result of the election of April 8, that the commitments made during that election should be honoured.
After all-and I say this without boasting -the electorate of the Atlantic provinces elected 20 members, out of the 33 from those provinces, to support the policies of the present government.
It would seem to me to be something of an affront to the electors in those provinces if those policies were now forgotten. I think the argument put forward by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton simply will not stand up. In the Atlantic provinces, we have had a decision of the supreme court of public opinion; and it is a pretty emphatic decision. I think that the resolution placed before this house by the Secretary of State will have to be supported.

We think the proposed amendments are in the right direction, perhaps hesitant steps but nevertheless going in the right direction; and as they tend to follow suggestions made in this house in the last session by members of this group, we are in favour of them.
Before I proceed to make the few observations I intend to make, perhaps I should say


something about my status, even to discuss questions which affect the maritime provinces. My constituency is in the middle of the industrial section of Toronto and it might be doubted that I should even dare speak on this subject. However, I learned to swim at the age of four in the bay of Fundy and I have vivid recollections of that. My grandfather happened to be the prime minister of one of the maritime provinces, so I think I should speak. I regret-and I say this without any disrespect to the present member for Cape Breton South-that the former member for Cape Breton South is not here so that his stentorian tones could be heard in this debate.
To return to the resolution: as I say, I think these are steps in the right direction. For example, the enlargement of the number of the members of the board was moved as an amendment in the last session of parliament by the former member for Cape Breton South and was opposed by all members of the house then present, with the exception of the members of this party. I am very happy to see that the government have studied what was then said and have adopted this suggestion. I commend to them that process as a general way of improving their legislation.
I think the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is wrong in suggesting that the proposal to enlarge the board in some way destroys its usefulness or significance. The purpose of enlarging the board, as we suggested in the last session, was to make it more representative not only of the different provinces but of the different economic groups in the maritime provinces. We are not particularly interested in whether the members are Liberals or Conservatives. All we hope is that they will be representative of business, labour, the professions and other groups who will be able to do an effective planning job. That is why we welcome this particular measure. We criticized the last bill because there was no capital fund made available. It is true that the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton said that the whole resources of Canada lay behind the implementation of the last bill, but we think it is a step forward to ensure that at least some of the $100 million is set aside for the purpose of seeing that this board can function effectively. Because it is absolutely ridiculous to talk of planning boards and to give them no means of operating. I heard the Secretary of State and the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough point out that this $100 million is only supplementary, but we feel that it is inadequate in any event.
I should like, Mr. Chairman, to refer to what my leader said in the last parliament

when this suggestion was made. He said that if expenditure of money helps to provide full employment and take people off the social welfare roll and off unemployment insurance, it will be the best investment the people of Canada ever made; so let us not begrudge expenditure of money like this. subtopic: STANDARD TRUST COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to incorporate Standard Trust Company. As has been indicated by the hon. member, Standard Trust Company was incorporated by parliament several years ago. Under the law a company so incorporated is required to commence business within two years. Standard Trust Company was not satisfied that it had been able to find within that period the management which it thought was desirable for the company and accordingly it did not commence business. It is now satisfied that it has both the capital and the management which are required and accordingly it is necessary to apply for the incorporation of the company again.
The bill has passed through the Senate and, of course, is now before this house. These trust companies provide a wide range of useful services to the community. They are subject to public regulation and control under the very detailed conditions and restrictions set out in the Trust Companies Act. The provisions of the bill now before the house are the usual. I believe they are selfexplanatory and require no detailed explanation. However, if there are any questions I will be happy to do my best to answer them.

subtopic: STANDARD TRUST COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it appears that in 1959 this bill, or a similar one, was introduced and we were led to believe that some of the problems to which the hon. member has referred were resolved at that time and the company was not only prepared to start operations then but was anxious to do so. We have noted that since that time the company has not begun operation and we also notice that there are a number of changes in the bill now before us from the one that was previously brought before parliament.
Before we go into some of those changes, and whether or not they are advantageous, I should like to refer to a broader matter that has to do with companies of this nature. It is one that has been widely discussed by the Liberal party in recent months and has to do with the Canadian composition of such companies and the Canadian element, so far as the shareholders, directors and money involved in the operation are concerned. You

Private Bills
will note, Mr. Speaker, that in this case the company incorporated in 1959 had two directors on its board who are not among the board of directors set forth in the bill now before us incorporating Standard Trust Company. They were Mr. Harry Willis residing at Belfountain, Ontario, a lawyer, and Mr. Murray Axmith, an executive, chartered accountant and director of a number of companies in Ontario.
I would presume that these two people were the executive officers who were going to administer the company and I am surprised that they have been removed without any replacements being suggested to us. We agree with those in the Liberal party, and I think they are in the majority, who believe that there should be greater control of a Canadian companies by Canadians, that we should have available to us Canadian trust companies that will provide the services this company is seeking to provide and that we should be assured that the shareholders and directors are Canadians and that the shares are owned by Canadians.
I am aware of the fact, of course, that the statutes of Canada make it mandatory that in any company of this nature incorporated under the Trust Companies Act the majority of the board of directors must be normally resident in Canada and be either Canadian citizens by birth or by naturalization. I suggest that we should be assured and that it should be set forth in the bill that all the directors of this company must be Canadians normally resident in Canada. I suggest we should also go further and ascertain whether or not the shareholders are Canadians and whether or not the stock is under the control of Canadians.
I question that this is true in this case because I am aware that one of the proposed directors of this company is also a director of a number of companies whose shares are widespread, and it is difficult to ascertain from a quick perusal of these companies whether or not they are actually controlled in Canada. If we are going to do as the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and former adviser on the economic development of Canada has said, and buy Canada back, I suggest it is essential before starting to do so that we direct that any company incorporated under the Trust Companies Act should meet these requirements in the initial stages. I suggest that we should be told, not only with regard to this company but other companies as well, that this matter has been considered with the result that these companies are truly Canadian.
We should like to suggest to the members of the other place that when these bills are referred to their committee a great deal of

advantage could accrue to this house if their proceedings were recorded. In that way the discussions and deliberations of the banking and commerce committee of the other place would be made available to members of this house. It may be repetitious for us to have to ascertain facts that may have previously been made known in the other place, and for what it is worth I make the suggestion that the banking and commerce committee of the other place keep a record of its proceedings so that this information will be available.
It will be noted from the bill that the company will have a capitalization of $5 million whereas in the 1959 bill the amount sought was only $3 million. This money will be contributed by subscription, I presume, and no doubt very large sums will come from some of the companies with which the proposed members of the board of directors of this company are connected. This raises a very difficult problem. I will only refer to the director who I know is connected with the mining industry. Many of the mining companies are holding companies which delegate their authority down the line and as a result it is very difficult to ascertain where the ownership of this company will really lie.
I suggest that the committee should give very serious consideration to ascertaining the facts in relation to the Canadian composition of this company before we give any consideration to the passing of the bill. I am sure that other bills of a similar nature will be brought before the house in which similar powers will be sought. Parliament in the past has seen fit to enact the Trust Companies Act and I should like to refer particularly to section 19 where I find these words:
The majority of the directors of the company shall at all times be persons resident in Canada and subjects of Her Majesty by birth or naturalization.
In my view this was a very forthright and forward step, and having in mind that we are having difficulty in controlling our own economy from the point of view of the companies that operate in Canada I think that this kind of commitment should be made to the house when the incorporation of any such company is sought. I think the sponsor of the bill has an obligation to the house to give us some information with regard to why this company did not proceed to operate. The bill incorporating this company was passed in 1959, and I feel there is an obligation on the sponsor of the measure before us to tell us why the company did not proceed to operate in the normal manner during the last four or five years.
A limitation of two years was set by parliament as the time within which such a company should commence operations. This

provision was enacted for the protection of the general public. I believe that there has been a circumvention of this provision and the members of the house should be made aware of the reasons this company did not proceed with its intentions. I believe that in setting up the original board of directors there was an attempt to obtain men with business administration ability. There was a lawyer appointed; but it may be debatable whether or not this is any protection to the shareholders of a trust company in the province of Ontario. However, I believe that was the intention. Then, too, there was the appointment of an accountant to the board of directors, a man of whom it was said at the time that he was a chartered accountant, an executive and director of a number of companies in Ontario and a resident of the township of Etobicoke. These two gentlemen, it would seem to me, formed the business side of this trust company. The other people were well known figures, including several cattle breeders, a well known grain operator in the province of Ontario and a well known real estate operator in the city of Toronto, as well as a former member of the Ontario legislature and a former cabinet minister.
These people are members of the new board of directors, and personally I can see nothing wrong with that. I do believe that these people may lack the business sense that was associated with the establishment of the original board of directors. However, on the earlier occasion a point was made of establishing a board containing people of administrative ability such as a chartered accountant or practising lawyer.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these are questions that should be answered. Why was this company unable to raise the necessary money to commence operation? We were told that they would be able to do so in the very near future. A statement to this effect will be found on page 863 of Senate Debates for June 18, 1959. I quote:
In the bill it is proposed that the capital stock of the company shall be $3 million, which may be increased to $5 million if such an increase is found necessary.
It is interesting to note that before this company ever starts operations, the new company has found it necessary to ask for $5 million, even though the old company did not obtain the $3 million necessary to commence operations. I continue to quote:
Honourable senators will note from clause 4 of the bill that $500,000 must be subscribed before the provisional directors can call a general meeting of shareholders for the purpose of organizing the company. This, I understand, conforms with the provisions of the Trust Companies Act.

Furthermore, the bill provides that even after the sum of $500,000 has been subscribed the company shall not commence business until $1 million of capital stock shall have been subscribed and at least $1 million paid thereon.
From information furnished to me I understand that it is the present intention of the sponsors of this bill to provide that $1,100,000 shall be paid for the first $1 million of capital stock which shall be subscribed for and issued, the purpose of this being to immediately provide this company with a capital surplus of $100,000. As all honourable senators well know, a trust company loses money when it first commences to do business, and the sponsors feel that rather than have the capital of the company impaired by a loss which the company will incur when it commences business, the company will be provided with a capital surplus of approximately $100,000, and any loss which may be incurred can be charged against the capital surplus account.
I understand from the sponsors that they are in a position to immediately provide the trust company with stock transfer business which should produce an annual income of approximately $100,000 for the company.
This statement, Mr. Speaker, was made by the Hon. Senator Brunt during his remarks when he introduced the bill which was subsequently passed by the Senate and this house. However, four years later this company has not been able to raise the original million dollars. They have not been able ta form the company and an indication has been given to the house that they have not even raised the $500,000 necessary before a meeting of the shareholders can be called.
I feel these matters are of prime concern to the house in the establishment of a trust company. It would seem to me that, if this company cannot live up to the trust we have already put in it when the bill was before us in 1959, then it should not be called a trust company at all. There is an indication that if the name of the company is not suitable to government officials and the banking and commerce committee decides to change it, the company would be agreeable. If that is so, we could call it something other than a trust company.
I believe that this is a matter of great importance. If we are given to understand that certain things will be done, certain responsibilities carried out in an area over which we have complete jurisdiction, then I believe we are entitled to a full explanation as to why these things have not been possible. We should be told why the company did not proceed as it originally intended, why certain people have been dropped from the board of directors, why the board of directors does not now contain persons of recognized ability in certain fields such as accounting and law.
I should like to see the house consider this bill, if that is its wish, but I should like to see the bill considered on the basis of the fact that the company has already failed

to live up to the obligations it assumed upon obtaining its original charter. Then, too, we should give consideration to the argument that a trust company incorporated in Canada should have a provision in its charter to the effect that Canadian ownership of that trust company will be maintained. This provision should apply not only to the board of directors but to the shareholders as well.
Certainly the day has now arrived when we are in a position to do something on our own behalf about some of these companies. I believe there is a growing desire for us to have companies that are completely Canadian, that will concern themselves with Canadian problems and with meeting Canadian conditions. I suggest this will not happen if the majority of the money is brought in through mining companies that may not be controlled in Canada, or through other organizations most of whose stock is held outside Canada.
There can be an acceptance of the principle of Canadian ownership and operation of companies only when we in the parliament of Canada are willing to amend our own legislation to that effect. I suggest that the bill be not read now and that it be referred back, not to the committee but to the sponsor himself, so that he can give further consideration to some of these problems, and later present it again to the house, having taken into account some of the problems that are very important to the passing of this particular bill.
