Before we proceed to come to a conclusion about this bill there are some points I would like to mention, following along the general tenor of the remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). We believe that all necessary steps should be taken to ensure that the corporate structure in Canada is Canadian owned all the way across the board and all through its operations, and that lip service alone is not sufficient, such as has been the case in the past few years.
The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) introducing the bill indicated that this company is different in so far as the members of the initial board of directors are concerned, and different in one other aspect about its capitalization; but he also said the company was in fact incorporated by private bill some four years ago in 1959. So far as the Senate was concerned it was incorporated again during the last session of parliament, but with the intervention of dissolution it did not proceed through this chamber.

I gather that the persons who are listed as being the petitioners, and who in fact will be the provisional directors of this company, are at the moment Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada. Their names are given in clause 1 of the bill, and also their occupations and addresses, which I understand are all in Ontario. This in itself is laudable. This is something we all like to see, Canadian citizens participating in the formation of companies and the development of our industries. But while they may be at present Canadians there is no guarantee anywhere in the bill that such will always be the case, except in so far as the provisions of the Trust Companies Act apply, which requires that all such companies shall have Canadian citizens as the majority of their directors. Actually "British subjects" I think are the words in the Trust Companies Act, and this has been dealt with by the hon. member for Timiskaming.
To us this is the key point we should be looking at in so far as the incorporation of this particular company is concerned. We should be looking at this and other similar companies from the point of view of Canadian ownership so far as capital is concerned, and as members of parliament we should be seeking to give full effect to the desire that rests in all hon. members to develop and promote Canadianism, and Canadian ownership and control of corporations in Canada, using our resources and finances.
Two years ago we had quite a lengthy debate in parliament concerning a similar subject matter. It was a pipe line company, Aurora Pipe Lines Limited, and at that time it took a considerable amount of discussion, debate, crossfire and argument to get the sponsor of the legislation and the company which was to be incorporated to agree that all directors of the company should at all times be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada. It took many weeks of debate to achieve that, and I hope such will not be the case in this parliament. I hope that principle and concept will be readily agreed to by the people who are petitioning for the incorporation of this company, and that they will be agreed to by the sponsor of the bill.
For many years our predecessors in politics, the C.C.F. party, advocated and campaigned on the concept and principle of Canadian ownership and Canadian control of our industry. It was not too many years ago when that idea was ridiculed and pooh-poohed by other political parties, and especially by people in the business world. But gradually, arising from the principle advocated by the C.C.F. party, there has come to be an understanding and appreciation on the part of all

political parties that we must do something to regain control of our own industry and our [DOT]own economic destiny.
Ours is no longer a lone voice arguing this particular principle of Canadianism. Four or five years ago we were joined by the Conservative party. Admittedly at that time it was bent solely and simply on getting into [DOT]office, regardless of how it got there through promises; but nevertheless in 1957 it did embrace the concept of Canadian ownership and control. It is true also that following its attainment of office it did not do very much to put that concept into effect. Now we have the Liberal party in office. At one time it objected strenuously to the ideas we expressed and which we promote now. But we do have articles written and comments made by the present Minister of Finance, before he became minister, about the objectives we must have and the steps we must take to develop Canadian ownership of industry and other economic activities in this country. In fact, there appeared in the Weekend magazine published during the election campaign a very extensive article written by one Walter Gordon. The article was entitled "We must buy back Canada", and the subtitle was, "The Liberals' expert on business gives his recipe for independence". I might add as an aside that it did not give his recipe for independence from Toronto businessmen and financiers, but none the less I presume it gave his recipe for the economic independence of Canada. The article indicates who Walter Gordon is; it gives his background in so far as being chairman of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects is concerned, and similar information.
In this article the Minister of Finance- of course, he was not then the minister- goes into great detail, although not as great as one would wish, about the degree of foreign investment in Canada dating back to 1900. He shows the tremendous growth, in billions of dollars, of total foreign investment in Canada since that time, from just a little over $1 billion in 1900 to something more than $22 billion in 1960. He indicates the percentage of foreign ownership and control of selected industries in Canada, going back to 1954 in this instance. But throughout this article-and I do not intend to quote sections from it-the person classified as the Liberals' expert on business who is giving his recipe for Canadian economic independence, presumably, talks about the degree of foreign ownership and control of Canadian industry, the damaging effects this has upon our economic growth and the steps which are necessary to overcome this situation. We agree with what the Minister of Finance
Private Bills
wrote in that article in so far as the damaging effects of foreign ownership and control upon Canadian industry are concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief reference to a governmental publication in support of the attitude expressed by the Minister of Finance in that article. The publication from which I quote was referred to in a previous parliament. It is the Canadian Balance of International Payments, 1960, and International Investment Position, a publication of the dominion bureau of statistics. I quote from page 58 of this official government publication on the growth of foreign control and investment in Canada:
Perhaps the most striking feature of these series,-
This is referring to the series of statistics:
-viewed in the perspective of a third of a century, embracing depression and boom, war and peace, is the consistency of the direction of the changes. Foreign ownership of Canadian manufacturing has inched up from 38 per cent in 1926 to 51 per cent in 1959 and control has gone from 35 per cent to 57 per cent. Foreign ownership of mining and smelting has also reflected an almost uninterrupted growth from 37 per cent in 1926 to 59 per cent in 1959 and control has risen from 38 per cent to 61 per cent. Apart from these industries there has developed a substantial petroleum and natural gas industry which is 63 per cent foreign owned and 75 per cent foreign controlled.
The dominion bureau of statistics figures are from 1926 which, as I understand it, was the year the d.b.s. started to compile statistics of this sort. These statistics show that from 1926, at least, until 1959, which is the last year for which I have the figures, there was a steady, uninterrupted, year by year increase in the degree and percentage of foreign control and ownership of Canadian industry. What it does not say, and what I am sure everyone realizes, is that from 1926 until this very day, unfortunately, we have had either a Liberal or a Conservative government in office in Canada and it did not particularly matter in those years who was in and who was out, the growth was the same; the give away of our resources to foreign interests was identical whether there was a Liberal or a Conservative government in office. It was during the later years to which these statistics refer that, as I said earlier, those in the C.C.F. party were campaigning both at election time and in this house-I refer to my predecessors here in the C.C.F. party-for a return into Canadian hands of the control of our economic destiny. It was during those years that the Liberals and the Conservatives, whether in government or in opposition, turned a deaf ear and refused to listen. This was the situation up to a couple of years ago. As a result, we are now stuck with the inheritance of the blindness of each of these old line parties on this

Private Bills
question of owning and controlling our economic activity and destiny. This economic independence is what we are trying to accomplish.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, at one time both the old line parties objected to this course of action. At one time they refused absolutely to concern themselves with whether the growth of foreign ownership was damaging or otherwise to Canadian interests. They refused absolutely to even study the question, and only in the last four or five years were any public pronouncements made by either the Liberals or the Conservatives about this all important question which now confronts us. It confronts us in the bill that is before us; it does not only confront us as a general proposition. It does not only confront us in so far as our manufacturing industry is concerned, the mining and smelting industry, the petroleum and natural gas industry or any other industry. This question of foreign ownership and control confronts us perhaps even more in the field of finance, in the field of control over interest rates, the operation and issuance of currency, credit and the like. I refer to the field of banking, the financial structure of Canada, the trust and loan companies field, the mortgage field and the like.
We have before us just one small part of the problem which concerns us. That small part is Standard Trust Company, an act to incorporate this body. While it may be a rather small company, only one company, and some may consider that it is just a small part of the total trust and loan company picture in Canada and an even smaller part of the total financial interests in Canada, nevertheless we must start to deal with this problem at some point. I suggest this is the point at which to start, when the issue comes before us.
The capital stock of the company is established as being $5 million. I have here the report of the superintendent of insurance for Canada for the year ending December 31, 1961. In it there are listed 15 trust companies in Canada. I presume there are only 15 trust companies in Canada, although I may be inaccurately informed-I may have been misreading the information in this report. The report is not particularly voluminous, it is true, but none the less it is filled with statistics.

I should like to say one or two words on the bill. We certainly do not wish to hold the bill up in any way because we think it should go to the

committee where it could be studied in detail and where the interested parties could appear and give evidence.
We want to get on with the business of the house so that this measure may be referred to the appropriate committee for more careful consideration. I understand, in any case, that in sending such a bill as this to a committee we are not, really, endorsing the principle of the measure; I think we were told that in the last parliament. Bills such as this are allowed to go forward on a second reading for a more detailed study. However, there are some doubts I wish to express at this stage in order that the sponsors may give consideration to them before the bill is considered by the committee.
Previous speakers from this party have stated that our main concern in these matters is to try to build into the bill itself sufficient safeguards to ensure that these various financial companies which we are incorporating shall not at some later date pass into the hands of people who reside outside Canada. I have read over the names of the provisional directors. These are, of course, only provisional and they will change at a later date. Some of these names are familiar and they appear to belong to excellent individuals. At the same time, it is not sufficient to have as a majority of the directors people who are normally resident in Canada. This ensures, of course, that the Canadian point of view is available to the company at all times. We are more concerned however with the idea of Canadian control, and this does not necessarily follow merely because the majority of directors will be people resident in Canada.
It is more important to build into the bill some safeguards attached to the actual stock of the company, its eventual distribution and the hands into which it will finally pass. We are making these observations at this point to suggest to the sponsors of the bill that some consideration be given to revising the capital stock of the company so that the majority of the common shares will always be held by Canadian citizens. If this is done we need never fear that control of the company will pass into hands outside our borders. This is in no way discourteous or unfriendly to people outside Canada. They are probably all good businessmen. But we feel that as a matter of the good, practical running of the country, institutions of this type should always remain under Canadian control.
As other hon. members have pointed out, these institutions are often small in the beginning-though I notice that this one has a capital of $5 million. As they continue to

operate in the community they acquire substantial assets. Trust companies, in particular, are now spreading out into the banking field in Canada and taking deep root in the monetary community. I recall that in the last parliament we had a measure before us seeking to incorporate the Allstate Life Insurance Company. Objections were raised then to the effect that this company, from its inception, would be 87 per cent owned by a United States company. We objected to this at the time and asked that consideration be given to revising the capital set-up so that the controlling shares would remain in Canada. This suggestion was enthusiastically received by the sponsor of the bill, and I understand consideration was being given to that proposal. However, parliament dissolved and we were not able to revive that measure. I know this is a reasonable proposal, and perhaps it would find favour with sponsors of the present measure.
What we are discussing here goes to the root of the Canadian economy and to the main problem facing it, which is the continuing drift of Canadian resources into hands outside our borders. It is not necessary, I am sure, to repeat the difficulties which this creates for a community-the problems of planning and the handicaps to the intelligent running of our economy. I think it is true to say there is no country in the modern world which has permitted as large a proportion of its natural resources to be controlled from outside its borders as has Canada. That is why we are trying to serve notice that in all these bills we are anxious to see that safeguards are built in to see that at some time in the future control of policy and shares will not pass into hands outside Canada. It is often said that by taking this attitude we are limiting the desire of people outside our borders to invest in Canada. Of course, no one wants that to come about, because capital from outside sources is still needed. However, examination of the capital available in Canada indicates that this fear is exaggerated. Many sources of development capital are available within our own borders, but no real attempt has been made to marshal this capital. We are told that a measure will be brought before the house designed to meet this difficulty. If that is true, and if the necessary capital funds are made available, we need have no fear about building into measures of this kind the safeguards which spokesmen for our party are suggesting this afternoon. If the capital is available in Canada there need never be any fear of getting into difficulties with groups outside the country.
These are all the observations I have to make at this time. As I say, we do not want to delay the measure unnecessarily, though we

do wish to emphasize to other members who are sponsoring these pieces of legislation that we intend to do every thing we can within the rules to ensure that financial institutions and corporations set up by this parliament will be so established that the control of their policy and assets will remain in the hands of Canadian citizens in perpetuity.

I pointed out, however, that even though the Secretary of State and the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough both said that the fund of $100 million was only a supplement, we in this party seriously doubted its adequacy. It is our view, Mr. Chairman, that adequate capital expenditures are essential if the economic planning for the maritimes is to be on a scale that will enable these provinces to reach permanently a situation of economic welfare on a parity with the rest of Canada. Perhaps the reason can be found in the article, something that Brigadier Wardell had to say about the former government and what they anticipated when they appointed him. Perhaps it was this expectation that was the reason for the suggested enlargement in the membership of the Atlantic development board. This is what he had to say:
Indeed, I always felt that the very fact of my appointment was evidence of the previous government's intention to go the whole way in the application of the remedies-
The remedy he is talking about here is not this $100 million. He is talking about $4 billion. I say that $100 million is a piker's approach to the problems of the Atlantic provinces.
Why did you not say so last year?

Because I did not have to say so; we had the treasury of Canada behind us. Brigadier Wardell went on to say this:
I have campaigned for years to demonstrate the formidable scale of attack. I, and the publications I control, have always been completely independent politically. I should have been the last person the government would have chosen if they were not meaning to carry the policy through to its ultimate conclusion.
What better evidence, Mr. Chairman, than the words of the man we appointed to be the chairman of the Atlantic development board that we were going to spend a billion dollars in the next ten years if we had remained the government?
Why did you not put it in the bill?

We did not have to put it in the bill. We had the federal treasury available to the Atlantic provinces, all the money for all the projects that you could possibly anticipate. Since the hon. member is talking

about money, I might ask him: what is $100 million going to do for the Chignecto complex when it would take $350 million to build the dams alone? Are you willing to support the construction of the Chignecto complex and the Chignecto canal? The hon. member is shaking his head. He does not support the construction of the Chignecto complex.
Not out of these funds.
I am glad to hear the hon. member for Westmorland say he does not support it.
Not out of these funds.

That is quite a revelation; it will be quite a revelation to the people of Westmorland. This is all the more reason for feeling that the Chignecto canal committee should meet, and meet early to find out what this government is going to do with this project, now that Liberal members are standing up and saying they are opposed to it.
Why did you not do something about it?

I should like to know what more I could have done, unless it was taking a spade and going out and digging the ditches myself. I would have been willing to do that if I thought it would have accomplished anything.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have had some very helpful remarks from the members on the opposite side. I hope we will have some more. I look forward-
Speed it up a little.
The gentleman says, "Speed it up a little". I say to him that he will not say, "speed it up a little"-
Yes, we will.

If you can speed up anything that would accomplish something for the Atlantic provinces, rather than the destruction of the Atlantic development board, then I will be happy to hear from you. Until then, I suggest perhaps you should stand on your own two feet, do your own talking and put your own proposals before this house.
Now, I should like to make a few comments on this letter the Secretary of State wrote to the chairman. I quote from it, in part:
The board will have the responsibility of recommending the expenditure of this fund and of supervising such expenditures, but the final approval of each capital project rests with the government.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State just how these projects will finally be approved? Will it be by the cabinet or the House of Commons, or by the premier of
Atlantic Development Board Act Newfoundland? If it is to be by the cabinet, then let's face it: all we are doing is providing a patronage fund of $100 million for the Liberal party in the Atlantic provinces, and I do not think anybody in the Atlantic provinces wants that sort of set-up.
There are other questions I would like answered. I would like the Minister of Labour to say whether he approves of the demotion of Frank Sobey, who was vice-chairman with a four year appointment, to an ordinary member for one year? I would like to know whether the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough approves of Frank Sobey's dismissal from the board, because that is what it is. I would like to hear from the other members from the Atlantic provinces to know if they approve of such actions.
This is the lowest type of political partisanship that could possibly be found anywhere, and I feel that the Atlantic provinces deserve something better than that. If that is what we are to look forward to receiving from the Liberal government then, while the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough pointed out that they had 20 Liberals from the Atlantic provinces last time, I venture to say they will have none when the next election comes around.
There are many other aspects of the measure that are of particular importance to hon. members from the Atlantic area. I should like to know whether the Secretary of State has consulted and personally written the various members of the board to tell them their term was going to be reduced to one year. I realize he has written the chairman, and the chairman is aware of this, but I would like to know if the other members have been advised.
I would also like the Secretary of State to inform me whether he is planning on advising the provincial governments about the six further appointments that are to be made to the board, something which he suggested in the last parliament we should do. I would also like to know if the Secretary of State really believes the gentlemen we appointed, the ablest men available in the Atlantic provinces, are not just remaining on this board because they do not want to get into a public fight with the government of the day over its political partisanship. You, know, Mr. Chairman, I find it hard to think of a word sufficient to describe how low an act it is and still use parliamentary language.
How about the word "Liberal"?

Atlantic Development Board Act found. Fifty or sixty years ago this type of attitude might have been acceptable, but it is not the type of approach we look forward to in the Atlantic provinces now. We look forward to the type of approach that will get us the ablest men it is possible to find, no matter what their political beliefs might be, and band them together to do the very best they can for the area. And, Mr. Chairman, it is quite a job, even when we do find the ablest men.
We have a big task before us. It has been indicated it will take $4 billion to bring the Atlantic provinces even close to the level of the richer provinces of the country. It is felt that $1 billion should be injected into the maritime economy within the next 10 years, and if this $100 million which the Secretary of State suggests as a fund were available each year, then I would say we would have a pretty satisfactory fund and we could not do very much arguing about it.
I do not like the principle of giving moneys to boards. I do not like the principle of taking the power away from parliament, of selecting the means by which public money is spent, even if it were $100 million a year. But, Mr. Chairman, it is not $100 million each year for the next 10 years. It is $100 million for six or seven years, and it will probably be five years by the time they get the board working. After that time the government will kill the board, as the former minister of national revenue said. The Liberals are going to bury it, and now they will have six Grit pallbearers to go along to the funeral.
One hundred million dollars is an infinitesimal amount of money when one looks at what the former government did when it was endeavouring to lift up the economy of the area. In Atlantic adjustment grants alone we provided $275 million. There were many other acts by the former government. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton mentioned the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, and there was the Beechwood act. There are many examples where we poured millions of dollars into the economy of the Atlantic provinces, but it still requires hundreds of millions of dollars more. It will not get them from this board.
There has to be some other approach to this matter if we are really going to get the type of incentive, the leap forward, which the Secretary of State spoke about last night. "We are in low gear with $100 million, and we will never get out of low gear if we only have $100 million. Last night the Secretary of State told me that the government is providing more money under the Trans-Canada Highway Act. I think that is just great. Certainly I am not against it in any way, shape or form.

I think the Secretary of State owes the Atlantic provinces an explanation with regard to these six new appointments. The hon.

member for Greenwood mentioned the fact that last year the Secretary of State and the Liberal party voted against an amendment proposed by his party to enlarge the Atlantic development board. He says he is glad to see they have come around to his party's way of thinking and are going to enlarge the board. There is no better reason than that.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman seems to have patronage on the brain.

There is a very good reason for my having patronage on the brain, because I know who will appoint and who is going to be running the Atlantic development board. There is no better reason in the world than the examples we have had that the hon. member has patronage on the brain and is in a position to do something about it.
Where is the brain?

The hon. member for Saint John-Albert is less kind to the Secretary of State than I am. I think he has some brains, but he thinks the people in the Atlantic provinces have fewer brains than they in fact have, otherwise he would not have brought in this type of resolution to enable him to do his political partisan work. I think I have said enough on this occasion, Mr. Chairman.
Hear, hear.

I can well understand that they do not like it when they hear the truth. It is too bad the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not here to lead them on another crusade for the truth, but unfortunately it is the type of truth that has the political partisan bias that we are getting in sufficient amounts in the legislation that has been proposed today.

Mr. Chairman, during the debate this afternoon and again this evening a number of official opposition members have challenged Atlantic provinces members to make known their position on the proposed amendments to the act which established the Atlantic development board. I trust that in making known my position I can do so with the dispatch that I am looking forward to and that I am sure all hon. members would like to see attend the passage of these amendments in order that we may get on with the
Atlantic Development Board Act job. My opinion can be expressed in this way, and I think it is one that is widely shared in the province of Nova Scotia. The composition of the present board does not provide the practical representation of areas and skills-* despite what hon. members opposite may have stated in this house today-essential to a balanced development program throughout the entire Atlantic region. By increasing the number of board members we provide an opportunity to correct this existing weakness which is apparent to anyone who is knowledgeable about the skills available in the Atlantic provinces. Indeed, it is only making invidious comparisons, which contribute nothing to this very essential undertaking at this time, to indulge in loud protestations about the skills of this or that individual.
We know how Industrial Estates operate in Nova Scotia; we know it is supposed to be and is in fact a non-political organization. We would like to see this board maintain itself in the same way. I think we can ensure this by increasing the number of members on the board. The provision of funds is the other essential feature of these amendments. This action inspires confidence that the social capital investment recommended by the board from time to time will not be sidetracked or delayed for some alleged austerity program or some other reason. The $100 million fund is a bond of good faith to encourage the maximum effort of the strengthened board in accomplishing its objectives within a reasonable time, and I trust that time will start within a few minutes this evening.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to speak on this measure, the first move designed and put forward by this government to cope with the special problems of our Atlantic region. I am happy to have heard those who have spoken. I would like to say to the hon. member from Greenwood that we maritimers welcome very much the contribution he made and the interest he showed. I welcome, too, the penchant for alacrity which the hon. member for Halifax has displayed this evening. Knowing his party, and being one familiar with its dealings with the mari-times for a quarter of a century, I find this a wholesome change.
I think the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton this afternoon, set a fine tone for this debate. He avoided partisanship, and indeed I think he went to extreme lengths in revealing the faith which he held for some of his fellow men who were not of his political party. I refer to his statement about the nonpartisanship of the Secretary of State and his confidence that he would not even be partisan in a geographic sense, let alone a political one. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is

Atlantic Development Board Act older and wiser than I. He may even be right. But I still commend him tor his faith. If any argument had to be advanced to indicate that the maritime region was grossly and shamefully neglected by the party in power between 1935 and 1957 in this country I would call as my first witness the leader of the Liberal party in the province of Prince Edward Island, a former premier of that province, who said "The St. Laurent government did not give us half a deal; Prime Minister Diefenbaker could do it. Why couldn't he?" Premier Matheson will remember very well the time when our little province was facing acute problems. The legislature was adjourned to allow him to come up to Ottawa to talk to his friends in the Liberal government and appeal to them for aid. He found that aid was not forthcoming. It would not be accurate to say he returned empty handed, because he did not. He returned with a bill for something like $1,250,000 which our little province owed to the dominion government because of some miscalculation in the dominion bureau of statistics-they had predicted we would be more fruitful and prolific than in fact we proved to be. The generosity of the dominion government was shown to this extent-that instead of having to pay the $1,250,000 in one fell swoop they allowed our little province to pay it back in five instalments. It reminds me of the farmer who, when advised by a veterinarian that he must cut off his dog's tail said he could not bear to do it all at once but would cut off a little bit every day.
Through the years this house has heard the pleas of the maritime representatives calling for a better deal. At times some of our political leaders became extreme in their views. They became so disturbed by the injustice of the situation that they suggested a political course of action which would have brought about the departure of certain parts of the country from confederation had that been possible. A notable example was when a former Liberal premier of Nova Scotia, the Hon. W. S. Fielding, rose to power in a repeal movement in 1886. He ended, of course, as a member of the dominion cabinet.
We in the maritimes have seen the fulcrum of economic power and advantage move ever further from us. I agreed with the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton when he said this afternoon that we do not want anything at the expense of the rest of Canada. I think, however, we can say that the prosperity of other parts of this country has in some measure at least, been derived from the disadvantages which we have had to endure for so long.
One has but to look over the record of the debates of this house and to have a mere

nodding acquaintance with history to know that on many occasions the needs of the maritimes have been bypassed. I was reading not long ago the record of the debates of 1912 when there was a great discussion about the northern territories, the resources of those territories and the extension of the boundaries of certain provinces. And Mr. Robert Borden, the leader of the Conservative party, reminded the house that there were other provinces which did not have northern territories but which had rights and claims.
We know how down through the years we have educated our youth and they have gone elsewhere. The story of maritime rights and maritime claims is not a new one. I shall not put it on the record again tonight. It is not for us here to relive past agonies and rekindle old grievances. Positive action and advancement to redress old wrongs is what is needed. I say with the greatest sincerity and with the greatest pride that no government ever moved so swiftly or so effectively to strengthen the maritime economy as did that government which took office in 1957. The Atlantic Provinces Adjustment Act was the first measure of aid and it was enacted within months and followed a commitment given by the Conservative candidates of the Atlantic provinces when they met in May, 1957, in Moncton. These commitments were honoured by the government in power. It is little wonder that at that time the leading Liberal organ of the province of Prince Edward Island, The Patriot, said about the adjustment grants:
The truth of the matter Is that this belated recognition of this island's fiscal need was long overdue by the government of Canada and that this province and the other Atlantic provinces as well are only now being treated a little more like the part of Canada that they are and less as poor relations.
This, I think, expressed the sentiment of the whole region.
What about term 29?

If the hon. member on my extreme left wants to look at the history of Newfoundland he will find that it was well treated by that same government.
After this measure of redress, and many others, the former government set up the Atlantic development board. There were improvements in our transportation system, new developments in our national parks and many other aspects of justice-I will not say generosity-on the part of a sympathetic and understanding government. We were given a new opportunity to engage in a program of self help. This was accomplished especially through the Atlantic development board, a fine piece of legislation which greatly cheered

the people of the Atlantic region and offered us new hopes and brought before us new vistas of opportunity.
I am not one who will say that because of the great things which were done between 1957 and 1963 all the ills of the maritimes have been cured. Far from it. We still have grievances. We have an average income lower by one third than the rest of Canada, double the unemployment and half the capital investment per capita. Therefore it is not surprising that even this government should take a special look at the problems of the Atlantic region, the oldest part of the dominion.
Someone said tonight that it was vain and futile talk to be assessing the personalities on the board. Leadership in the maritime provinces as elsewhere results from the human potential. The board which was set up was a fine board. For years, we in the maritimes have exported our able people. We have educated some of the finest scholars in the world and because of the lack of opportunity at home they have had to go elsewhere. It used to be a saddening exercise to look over the calendars of the universities in this country, in the United States and Great Britain and find hosts of maritimers there. A short while ago we had a reversal of the process. In Brigadier Wardell we found a man who came into the Atlantic region, saw these problems were solvable by united and vigorous action, and used the power of the press and the power of his own magnificent command of language to galvanize the thinking of people in the Atlantic region. And when he found a sympathetic response in a government which saw the facts of the maritimes clearly and was prepared to do something about them, he was given an opportunity to render great service. Now we discover that this man with his great comprehension of our problems, with his dedication to the solutions of these problems, is to be allowed to stay on the board as a member of the board for a couple of years. The hon. member for Cumberland, one of the outstanding members from the Atlantic region, referred to this famous letter from the Secretary of State. I will not read it again but I should like to refer to just one sentence:
The effective use of the fund will clearly require a close harmony of view between the government and the board and especially the chairman.
Thinking back, Mr. Chairman, over some of the events of the last few years I say that that is an ominous sentence, not only for Brigadier Wardell but for the Atlantic region.

speechtext: I can promise the hon. gentleman that if he will resign his seat I will be delighted to recommend to my colleagues that he be appointed to the board.

If the hon. gentleman is after my seat I think he would have to offer me at least a senatorship. If he wants to make the try I will make the resignation.
We have also on the board, Mr. Chairman, a distinguished representative from Prince Edward Island, Mr. Melvin McQuaid, the former provincial treasurer. When it is considered that he became provincial treasurer of a government which followed 24 years of Liberal administration and made a magnificent job of his task, I would say that he is pretty special and that a man like that would be a distinguished member on any such board. Mr. McQuaid would have to be classed, I would think, as a Conservative. The rest of the members of the board are Conservative appointees, that is true, and for this sin they are to be overwhelmed and smothered by six others. I will not refer to Mr. Sobey. His reputation in the industrial field and the progress achieved in Nova Scotia needs no adornment from any orator in this house or any member of either side of it. We are very proud of the director, the economist from Prince Edward Island who was brought in, Dr. Weeks.
You will have heard, Mr. Chairman, in recent days about the Bay street irregulars who have been assisting the Minister of Finance. I have not heard any mention of a specialist in the Atlantic economy or its problems being brought in, and having read some of the writings of the Minister of Finance I would have thought that this was the very area in which he most needed assistance and guidance. Having read the budget I am more convinced of that than ever. However, it is not for me to discuss the budget tonight. I will say only this, that the type of people appointed to the Atlantic development board did not deserve the kind of treatment they

Atlantic Development Board Act are about to receive through the enactment ol the legislation, the resolution of which is before us.
I do not think anyone will be greatly comforted by the assurance of the Secretary of State that Mr. Sobey, and I presume even Mr. McQuaid, will be eligible for reappointment under the tender mercies of this government. I should have thought that such able men who were prepared to take on this important duty on behalf of the Atlantic region should have been encouraged and told to carry on and go forward in their good work regardless of the political complexion of the government which appointed them. These men are taking on, and were prepared to take on, a major task, a task which has been challenging the Atlantic region for years and years, and I deplore this eager anxiety to smother, not a Conservative board because you could not call it that, but a Conservative-appointed board. And no one has yet advanced an argument which has convinced me that six more will make the board more representative. It will, I admit, make it larger, but not necessarily more representative.
My colleague from Cumberland and others have discussed this figure of $100 million. This sum of $100 million is offered as against nearly 100 years of neglect and injustice. If anyone feels that this will make a monumental impact upon the shrewd people of the Atlantic provinces, he is harbouring a dangerous delusion. A more realistic figure would be $4 billion. The former government was realistic and so deeply interested in the region that they did not lay down any ceiling on the amount. Not only is there a ceiling on the amount but there is a limitation on time as well. The limit is 1969, which gives five or six years to do the job. I do not think anyone will be taken in by this. I do not think anyone seriously believes that the great problems of the maritime provinces can be met, even if all these six people came from Bay street, in so short a time with so small an amount of money. All I will say-and like the Secretary of State I like to be nonpartisan about these things-is that while I am deeply disappointed, and I am afraid the people I represent will be discouraged, I will have to concede, considering the record of this government when it was in office before, that this is better than nothing, that is true. But it is not as good as was done before, and I submit, Mr. Chairman, it is not nearly good enough.
This strikes me as further evidence of the approach to great problems in this country which has already begun to characterize this government. It is a mere tinkering with the problem. The budget which will be discussed
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
is another exercise in tinkering. A tremendous facade is built up suggesting that a great new Atlantic board is being set up. I predict that after careful examination it will not only be revealed as tinkering but as bothersome and unhelpful tinkering as far as the economy of the maritime and Atlantic provinces are concerned.
Perhaps this is not too surprising. We never expected too great a kindness in the Atlantic region from this government because we remember some of the books written by the Minister of Finance and the statements he made before he wrote "Troubled Canada". We remember his recipe for maritime prosperity in those days-a little assistance to move us up to some other part of Canada. That was the recipe for the maritimes. This is not, nor never was, the attitude of this party. In 1956 the problems of the maritimes were discussed in this house. The leader of the Conservative party said at that time that "a full recognition of the moral obligation due to the Atlantic provinces, and a just arrangement with those provinces, is long overdue merely as a recognition of what was said at the time when those provinces came into confederation." This is where we stand, Mr. Chairman, and while I have no intention to obstruct, delay or hamper this tinkering effort, I will say again that in order to come close to their predecessors the government of the day will have to do much more.

Mr. Chairman, in the speech from the throne of September 27, 1962, we find on page 8 of Hansard a paragraph which reads:
You will be asked to authorize the establishment of an Atlantic development board to advise on measures and projects that will promote the economic development of the Atlantic region of Canada.
On November 19, 1962, the minister of national revenue of the day moved:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish an Atlantic development board and to define the duties thereof, to provide for the appointment of the chairman and other members of the board and for the payment of certain expenses of the members thereof, to provide for the appointment of an executive director of the board and for the payment of his remuneration, to provide further that the board may engage the services of such advisers and staff as may be necessary to enable it to carry out its duties and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.
And in December 1962, Bill C-94 received royal assent and became the Atlantic Development Board Act.

The resolution before us today is the sequel of appropriate legislation passed during the last session. This provision was invoked at the time as resulting from the report of a commission of inquiry on the economic prospects of Canada, which had been submitted in 1957. This was followed by five years of indecision, or even resistance, with regard to the protection and welfare of the Atlantic area.
Under defining clause 2, the term "Atlantic region", means the region comprising the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland.
I admit that this area requires special attention and study, particular measures and care. To this end, every one of us must give conscientious thought to the projects needed to increase, as far as possible, the standard of living of the people of that area which has been neglected for too long. I feel bound to point out at this time that the population of the lower St. Lawrence river, of the north and south shores and of the Gaspe peninsula should be considered without hesitation as part of the Atlantic area, when Bill No. C-94 is being amended and when some changes are being made in the administration of that act.
We, on this side of the house, do not believe in and are not obsessed with out-and-out industrialization. However, our area is considered by too many as a mere supplier of labour for industrial production.
Mr. Chairman, I endorse the words used by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) at the close of the speech he made in the house in that connection on December 4, 1962. Here is what he said on that occasion:
I would say again that the greatest need of this Atlantic area is for public capital that will bring to pass those particular public development projects which are necessary and which will assist in laying the climate and clarifying a situation that will attract our own capital in order that this country can go forward and that this area will not remain the depressed area, not the area which is the recipient of charitable welfare from the rest of Canada but the area which can and will lead the economic recovery our nation needs as it goes forward to fulfil our obligations not only to ourselves but to the generations which are to come after us.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that some day, the Bank of Canada will have a social capital service to provide, to supply the capital necessary to meet the requirements of the Canadian people, and in such a way that there shall be no inflation nor deflation and that unemployment, which is the lot of a startling proportion of our labour force in the lower St. Lawrence, in the Gaspe penin-

Atlantic Development Board Act sula and in the maritime provinces, shall be done away with forever through the good will of Canadian legislators. Do you not think that an economic problem, resulting from political policies, can receive a solution from the action of men animated by a constant desire to settle that problem?
The government has thought it necessary to raise from five to eleven the number of members on that board. I hope that all reasonable and equitable means will be taken to maintain the best men in their positions and that the increase in the number of members on that board will prove to be a refutation of political interference in the discharge of duties which go far beyond the temptation to make a political body out of such a board.
I wish that in the end we may come to a sound and healthy alliance between the various social elements in order to raise the people of the Atlantic area above their present financial and economic situation. It is our responsibility-all of us here share that responsibility and are aware of it-to change, transform or eliminate situations which aggravate the local people.
For a long time, as we all know, a complaint has been coming from the Atlantic area addressed to those who look after the business of the nation, and it is time now to act and to achieve the purpose of confederation.
As far back as 1926, the average income in the Atlantic area was 38 per cent lower than in the other Canadian provinces.
In 1955, our average income was still 37 per cent under the average for the other Canadian provinces.
To this date, in 1963, this problem has not yet been solved, even though I must admit that some individuals and institutions have to be commended for their efforts to solve it.
Is the economic development board determined to find a solution to those aggravating problems?
We certainly hope so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can think of no better occasion on which to enter the debates in this chamber in this twenty sixth parliament than this one, when consideration is being given to a resolution providing for amendments to be made to the Atlantic Development Board Act. As a member from Cape Breton island, the industrial heart of the Atlantic provinces, I may say that we looked upon this board as holding forth the promised stimuli that the economy in our area must

Atlantic Development Board Act have if we are to maintain that degree of growth that will provide sufficient employment for our citizens.
I listened with interest last evening to the explanations of the Secretary of State as to what he hoped the proposed amendments would accomplish. He did this in a very nice way, I must say, but I can only assume from his explanations that we will materially impair the operations of the board if the amendment to establish a fund of $100 million becomes a reality. One must compare this proposed fund with what is available to the board today. What we actually would be doing by establishing the fund is selling the resources of the federal treasury now available to the board for a maximum of $100 million, which is in effect placing a ceiling on the amount of federal participation in the Atlantic provinces over the next six years.
Even more alarming is the fact that the board is to expire forthwith on January 24, 1969, as has been mentioned by previous speakers and as indicated in the resolution. It is to expire, regardless of the fact the moneys in this fund may not be expended. This, however, is not a real danger. It is quite obvious that the funds that would be made available would easily be expended in a year and still not make the impression on the economy which, in the words of the Secretary of State, would result in a great leap forward. Indeed, experts who have made a close study of the needs of our area estimate that $4 billion would be needed over a period of ten years, with the federal treasury responsible for $1 billion of that amount.
If we were to use these figures as a guide-post, we would conclude that $100 million would be sufficient really for about one year. Instead, we find that the board has a fund of $100 million which will have to do for five years. Since it will take a period of time to determine which project should be proceeded with, and then a further period of time for this government to decide which project should be undertaken, we do not feel very hopeful.
The enlargement of this board obviously indicates a partisan approach to the selection of the members on the board. It can be expected, therefore, that this same partisan approach will apply in deciding which project will be approved.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if I could ask the hon. gentleman a question?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman, like his predecessors on the other side, has made a great play of this partisan approach to the


appointments to this board. Is this a reflection of a guilty conscience? Surely, the hon. gentleman would admit that if he thinks the appointments made by the previous government were not partisan there is no more reason to think our appointments will be partisan. What is more, I can assure him that they will not be.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Actually, the very brilliant and amiable member for Bonavista-Twillingate did not ask a question, he made a statement. Certainly, I have no guilty conscience, and I am sure the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton who guided this legislation through the last parliament has not a guilty conscience, either. Could it not be that there was a little urge pushing the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate? Could it not be that his conscience was bothering him? No, we do not have any guilty conscience. However, I was glad to hear from the minister that there will be no partisan appointments. This is a good commitment, coming from the Secretary of State.
If I may continue with my remarks, I should like to say that we can look forward to the $100 million as the maximum amount to be spent in the Atlantic provinces over the next five years. This will mean about $20 million per year divided amongst the four provinces. Compare this, Mr. Chairman, with the Atlantic adjustments grants which provide $100 million over a four-year period and will provide $175 million in the next five years. This program was instituted by the previous Conservative administration. The Atlantic provinces finally received some recognition after 22 years of neglect. We hope this recognition will continue unless the present government reduces or eliminates the assistance now available to this area from those grants.
The other day we heard comments in this house from the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister which indicated that perhaps we can look forward to a reduction in the subvention on coal. I hope there will be a clarification of this situation in the near future. I do not wish to go into that tonight, but I will deal with it on another occasion. Incidentally, I believe, if my memory serves me correctly that the subventions paid on coal by the Liberal administration during the fiscal year we came into power were in the vicinity of $8 million or $9 million. This year they will be $17 million. We have a little bit of stability in the coal industry today as a result of what has been done in that field by the previous Conservative administration.
Compare what you plan on doing with the announcement by Industrial Estates and the

Stanfield government a few days ago concerning the location of a $12 million cement plant in Nova Scotia. Compare it with the $40 million pulpwood operation located in Nova Scotia. I wish the hon. member for Halifax would speak a little louder if he has anything to say.

May I direct my question to the hon. member? I thought the Industrial Estates was cited as being associated with Mr. Sobey and a non-partisan board. What has this got to do with the subject under discussion?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: What has this interjection got to do with it? Is not Mr. Stanfield the premier of the province of Nova Scotia, or are you aware of that? Is not Industrial Estates Limited a board set up by that government?
That is where it stops so far as the government is concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Oh, yes, but there has been great co-operation between this independent board, Industrial Estates, and the Stanfield government. They have done an excellent job. I will go on to explain to the hon. member for Halifax, who apparently has not got his hearing aid turned up or apparently is not getting through, that he should compare this with the Volvo car manufacturing plant located in Nova Scotia by the Stanfield government or the carpet factory which was mentioned by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton this afternoon. One certainly does not have the feeling that the injection of this small amount of money is going to work economic miracles in the Atlantic area.
We compared these.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halifax made his great contribution for about two minutes, so I should like him to now sit on his brains and relax a bit.
I should like now to refer to Nova Scotia's representative, the vice-chairman of the board, Mr. Frank Sobey. I wonder if the hon. member for Halifax has anything against Mr. Sobey? I am glad he has nothing against him. If that is so, why did the hon. member not object in caucus to the Secretary of State because this legislation is practically giving this great man a year's notice, giving him a kick in the bottom. This is about the size of it. Why did the hon. member not object? Mr. Sobey is a man who has a deep love for his native province, Nova Scotia? Here is a man who is dedicated to advancing the economic interests of Nova Scotia. He is giving freely of his time and his great ability 28902-5-84
18, 1963	1313
Atlantic Development Board Act to promote industry for that area. He was successful in his own business, and has used a businessman's approach towards encouraging the establishment of new industries in Nova Scotia and the expansion of existing industries. This man is a member of the Atlantic development board, but if this legislation is implemented we are going to get rid of him. He has made a tremendous contribution to the welfare of his native province. Without any doubt, he undertook his duties as a member of the Atlantic development board in order that he may, in the future, give even greater service than he has in the past. The very fact that this man was a member of the board gave the people of Nova Scotia confidence that its operations would be a success.
Now, however, the services of this eminent Nova Scotian will be dispensed with. I can tell the government that this will not only mean a loss of confidence on the part of the people of Nova Scotia, but this board will be severely shaken. I have no doubt that if it were not for Mr. Sobey's dedication to the area he would have rejected, and with scorn, the proposal to limit his tenure of office. To the people of Nova Scotia this proposed action is contemptible and cheap.
Last night the Secretary of State, in his own inimitable fashion, spoke in grandiose terms of what the different departments of government will do in the Atlantic provinces over and above what the Atlantic development board might do; but, Mr. Chairman, for 22 years the provinces by the sea were neglected by a Liberal administration. However, after 1957 we were given greater attention than ever before, by a Conservative government. More expenditures by all departments of government were carried out in our area than ever before, and let me serve notice on the present government that we expect this to continue, and in fact increase, in addition to what the Atlantic development board may accomplish. To use the vernacular of the Secretary of State, that is to be a great leap forward. I did not know he was such an admirer of Mao Tse-tung until he used that phrase, but if this is not done it will not be a great leap forward. Rather it will be a great leap backward.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been watching the clock and I realize that if I do not say something now it will be at least a week before there will be an opportunity to do so. Some things have been said this afternoon that I think deserve a reply, and there are one or two questions to which I want to make a reply.
With respect to the first point made by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton I want to

Atlantic Development Board Act say with respect to the device used by the government-which of course I need not have revealed until the bill came up had I not wanted to be completely frank with hon. members at the start by making my letter to Brigadier War dell available to the committee -if the government had been so minded we could have done what the previous government did with the federal district commission when they substituted the national capital commission for it, and that was to legislate the old commission out of existence and the members with it, and appoint an entirely new slate. I may say no more partisan appointments were ever made by any government in the history of this country than were made to that commission by the right hon. gentleman who is now Leader of the Opposition.
Or, we could have done what the government did in 1960 at the time of the revision of the Canada Elections Act when, by a complete revision, it got rid of every returning officer in the country. But we did not choose to do that because we did not want to make this a partisan issue. We wanted to preserve continuity. I am sure the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton would admit at once, that when he came into the house and announced the appointment of the board in January, I welcomed the appointment of that board and I have never said one word at any time in criticism of any member of that board; and I have no criticism whatsoever to offer of any of them.
It is true that they were appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite; but that, in my view, is nothing against them and I would not hold that against them at all.
Would the hon. minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When I have answered the questions I have already been asked; but I have things to say and I would like to say them with a certain continuity, in fairness to the hon. gentlemen who have already spoken.
I have never at any time made any adverse criticism of any of the members of the board. The hon. member for Cumberland, who seems to be even more obsessed with this matter of partisanship than other hon. members opposite, asked me whether I had communicated with the other members of the board in addition to Brigadier Wardell. I have not communicated with them directly by letter, but I did give the letter I quoted last night to Brigadier Warded, the chairman of the board, whom I have seen several times since I became minister and whom I have tried to keep completely informed of what was going on. I may say, Mr. Chairman, I was very careful to observe the proprieties.

I did not discuss what we were proposing to do until the resolution was put on the order paper, but as soon as it was, I saw Brigadier Warded at once and told him precisely what we were planning to do, because I thought it was only proper, fair and courteous to do that.
I read my unsigned letter to him, and after he had read it I signed it. If Brigadier Warded had taken any exception to that letter I am sure any exception he would have taken would have been reasonable, and I would have done my best to modify it to suit him. Now, Brigadier Warded has spoken publicly, and the hon. member for Cumberland has quoted an article in a recent issue of the Atlantic Advocate. Brigadier Warded was good enough to let me have a copy of the speech he made to the maritime board of trade on June 4, before it was dedvered. He discussed the speech with me before he delivered it, in a general sort of way, but he never showed me the text until just before it appeared, and I made no suggestion as to what he should say in any way whatsoever. I think we can fairly assume Brigadier Warded, being an adult and a highly respected member of society and a highly self-respected person, meant what he said in what he said; and I would like to put on the record what he said in part:
First, let me summarize the resolution placed before the House of Commons on May 21 by Mr. Pickersgill.
This announced that the board's members would be increased from five to eleven; an Atlantic development fund of $100 million would be created for financing or assisting to finance programs or projects that would contribute to the growth and development of the economy of the Atlantic region and for which satisfactory financial arrangements are not otherwise available; that the board's life would end on January 24, 1969; and that the administration of the act would be changed.
Then he went on:
To comment briefly on these proposals, and 1 believe that I speak for the other members of the existing board-
I shall say a word about that in a moment.
-we shall warmly welcome the new members, and we shall do our utmost to work with them to the limits of our powers and in furtherance of the aims of the board.
As to the new terms of our appointments, we shall be glad to fall in with the government's proposals, whatever they may be, in substitution of the act of parliament by which we hold our appointments today. Personal considerations have no place in our minds. We are ready and happy to serve in any capacity.
I think I should pause here to say that when I gave my letter to Brigadier Wardell I asked him if he would send copies to other members of the board and point out to them I did not mark my letter confidential because

I thought I would want to read it to parliament; but I said in fairness to me as a member of parliament and so that I would not be accused by any member of contempt of parliament, I hoped he would not make it public until the matter came up for debate. He agreed to that very readily, and I said it was only fair he should send copies of the letter to the other members of the board so that they would know precisely what the conditions were, and I felt sure that if any of them wanted to communicate with me through him or directly they would do so.
The only member of the board I have met apart from Brigadier Wardell was Mr. Sobey, who called on me at my office in the House of Commons, and we had a very frank conversation indeed. He had not got the letter from Brigadier Wardell, and in fact I read it to him in my office and he said-you know he is a very frank fellow-"Would you like me to resign?" I said "No, I would not; I would like you to stay on the board; I want to preserve continuity. I want to keep this thing above partisanship. However, if we find at the end of the year that we do not like one another we do not need to continue this arrangement. If we do, we will."
He accepted that in the same spirit in which I gave it, and I do not think there was any misunderstanding of any kind between us. As the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton very properly pointed out, we as ministers have to take the responsibility for the expenditure of this $100 million, and whatever other hon. members think, such as the honourable and wealthy member for Queens, I still regard $100 million as a very large sum of money indeed, and I think most Canadians do. When we have to take the responsibility for the expenditure of $100 million it is absolutely essential that the agency through which it is expended shall have a harmonious relationship with the government. I am sure the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton would feel exactly the same way if he were standing in this position.
Yes; but may I ask the minister a question, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Does my hon. friend have any doubts about the harmonious relationship that this group of men would have with the present government, if they were continued in their present office?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, I have no doubts at all at the present time. But, as every hon. member knows, and certainly every hon. member who has served in a 28902-5-84J
