Atlantic Development Board Act cabinet, one may have the greatest possible feeling of respect and regard for another person and it may turn out that you cannot work well together. That often happens.
Would the minister permit another question?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Is this to be the attitude of the present government toward all boards?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, I would not think so. In the case of boards which have a statutory and quasi-judicial function. I would not think so. But this board is to exist for the purpose of spending public money for which the government in general, and I in particular, have to answer in this house. I think if anyone understands responsible government at all, it is essential that there be a relationship of harmony and confidence, and continuing harmony and confidence between the board, and particularly the chairman, and the government. I have no reason to think that this will not exist, none whatever. I am not suggesting there is any reason not to think so. There was the most complete frankness between myself and Brigadier Wardell, and a thorough understanding about the matter.
As to the question-and I might just as well deal with it now-of the additional membership on the board, Brigadier Wardell is a publisher. Mr. Sobey is fundamentally, as I understand it, a merchant, though he has many other interests; he is the director of a number of companies and is a man of very great substance and obviously of very great ability. The member from Prince Edward Island is an enforcedly retired politician, and I am sure all of us would feel sympathy for him. He was the provincial treasurer for a while until the electors decided they would rather have someone else for that particular seat. That is a risk we all run, but I do not think it makes him any less competent to serve on the board.
That has happened to members from that side too.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There were a number of people in the party opposite who are not here now. They fall in the same category.
Then let us not be so pious.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The member of the board from Newfoundland is a merchant in Water street. But when one looks at the economic complexion of the Atlantic provinces I do not think I could agree with hon. gentlemen opposite who say that the board should not be enlarged. I might mention that the fifth member is a banker. When you look at them, I do not think this group is very representative of the whole economic spectrum. There is no one

Atlantic Development Board Act from the fishery; there is no one from the great timber industry, which is the biggest of all the industries of the Atlantic provinces; there is not a coal miner or anyone representing the mining interests, and there is no one representing agriculture.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the minister accept a very small question on that point? I would like to ask him whether he would appreciate receiving recommendations from members of the opposition. For instance, would he like to have a member from Cape Breton island? Would he be prepared to accept such a recommendation ?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have always prided myself on having an open mind.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure that if the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria recommended a person who was in his opinion the best qualified person in Nova Scotia to serve on this board, he would be a person of eminence, integrity, and a good citizen. I do not think the hon. gentleman would recommend anyone otherwise, and I would of course be glad to have a recommendation from him. I cannot promise that I would accept it-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -but I would be glad to have it. However, I can assure all hon. members that in the recommendations I make to my colleagues and in the appointments, my colleagues see fit to make this board, the political complexion of the persons appointed will not be a factor at all.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What we will seek to do is get people who are representative of the main economic groups in the Atlantic provinces who are, in our opinion, best qualified to assist in the very important work of this board. I hope that the work of the board, notwithstanding some of the things that have been said this afternoon and this evening, can be lifted above partisanship and kept above partisanship. That is what we have every desire and every intention of striving to do.
I was asked whether we would communicate with the provincial governments about the persons to be appointed. I made a suggestion of that sort, perhaps a little sceptically, to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton when he was piloting the original legislation through the house. Perhaps this will be another precedent set by him that I will be inclined to follow. He is a pretty good example of the constitutional proprieties

in these matters. But there are, of course, four premiers in the Atlantic provinces; two of them are political friends of ours and two are political friends of hon. gentlemen opposite. I hope this board will work just as well with the Conservative governments as with the Liberal governments and that the cooperation will be just as good with the one as with the other. It is my intention, just as soon as the legislation has been passed, to write to the four premiers of the Atlantic provinces and ask them whether they would designate someone in the provincial administration, either a minister or an official, to act as liaison with the Atlantic development board, precisely so there may be that cooperation which we believe will be essential to the proper functioning of the board.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in the main objected to any amendment being made to the existing legislation. I can understand that position being taken by the hon. gentleman because he was the sponsor of the present act. It was his act, and I do not blame him for having pride of authorship. I think there is a lot of good in the act, and I said so at the time. We did not think it was as good as it could be and we said in opposition and during the election campaign that we thought we could make it better. As my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough pointed out before dinner, we said we would do two things, strengthen the board and give it a capital fund. That is what we went to the people and asked them to support us on. Does any hon. member on either side of the house expect us, having been elected and having elected 20 of the 33 members from the Atlantic provinces, to ignore that undertaking, not to carry out that commitment, to break that promise? We intend, if the house will agree-and of course we are in the hands of the house-to do precisely what we told the electors we would do, and we intend to do it in this session of parliament.
Whether it is right or wrong?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, we thought it was right or we would not have advocated it, and we advocated it in this house at the time the original legislation was put through. We considered it a deficiency, as the hon. member for Greenwood indicated he and his friends did, when it did not do these things. I feel sure that the hon. member for Greenwood is perhaps approaching the measure more objectively and in a less partisan spirit than are some hon. gentlemen opposite.
I say we are doing this in 1963, right after the election. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton was not elected to this house in 1957

but many of his friends were here. The hon. member for Cumberland was here. They were elected on a promise made at Moncton. In those hopeful days in May or June of 1957, the spring of the great promises, they promised a capital projects program to provide federal capital assistance for provincial projects designed to enlarge the basic economy of the area. That was in 1957. Three elections later, in 1962, as a deathbed effort they produced the Atlantic development board bill, without any capital fund. We do not intend to follow that example. As soon as this parliament will agree to it, we intend to do what we undertook to the electors to do. It seems to me that that is the only honourable course to take in the matter.
There has been a good deal of talk about a hundred million dollars being inadequate. The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria said it was a ceiling. It is the exact reverse. It is a floor. I think I should go back and quote Brigadier Warden's speech further on that precise point-his speech to the maritime board of trade.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Does he mean that if the hundred million dollars is used up in ten, 12 or 14 months parliament will provide another $100 million or $200 million?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, I am not parliament. I would not attempt to substitute myself for parliament. But I would hazard the guess that if we could get a board which was so dynamic and which could find enough projects to use this hundred million dollars up in six months it would be a lot better than the hon. gentlemen opposite did in six years. What is more, if the projects on which it was being spent were of the kind which this house and the people of Canada felt would contribute to the raising of the whole level of the economy of the Atlantic provinces, no government would have any trouble about getting more from this parliament, if more were needed to carry on that task. I have no doubt about that whatsoever. But $100 million, I suggest, is $100 million more than nothing, and it is a good start.
Here is what Brigadier Wardell said on June 4 on this point:
As to the $100 million fund and the limitation of the life of the board to five and one half years, the amount is but a tenth of the billion dollars previously envisaged for a ten-year period, but which, of course, was never actually specified.

The tidal power element in the Chignecto project alone, so near and dear to this area, would cost $350 million and take ten years to complete. The $100 million fund would only provide $4.5 millions per province per year during the life of the board.

I wonder if the minister would check the accuracy of his remarks before he makes them in future.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I will leave that to the hon. member. I think my remarks were accurate and I think the ordinary principles of British justice should operate and that I should be considered innocent until I am proven guilty.
Does the minister think I would bring the matter up if I did not think I could prove him wrong?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, a moment ago I was about to read a further paragraph from Brigadier Warden's letter, but before I do so I do not think I can let pass the observation made by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. I do not think it was characteristic of the hon. member, who is usually not among the more partisan members opposite-I reciprocate the compliment he paid me earlier today-but who I think in this case was really extraordinarily unfair. There seems to be an impression in this house that anyone on the opposite side of the house is able to make as partisan and strong a speech as he likes, and that everyone on this side has to sit and like it and enjoy it without complaint, and if any reply is made in kind hon. gentlemen at once suggest that is unfair and is an excuse for prolonging a debate which they would not otherwise prolong. I am sure that on reflection the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton will realize that the purpose of debate is not to run a sort of Sunday school; that the purpose of debate is to debate, and that surely we should be able to debate in this house like adults without getting sore about it.
Your memory is too short.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the minister that the time allotted to him has expired.
Continue.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should just like to read this one other paragraph from the letter of Brigadier Wardell because it seems to me it should be part of the record.
But my understanding is-
Are you looking for inspiration?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When the former Speaker has called me to order once more perhaps I may proceed.
But my understanding is that the $100 million does not at all limit the special aid to the Atlantic region to that amount in the next five years.
I would draw that to the attention of hon. members. This is Brigadier Wardell speaking.

The qualifying phrase in the resolution is in the following words: "financing or assisting in financing programs or projects .. . for which satisfactory financing arrangements are not otherwise available."
The Atlantic development board's special fund will be used as a special supplement to the funds provided by the activities and programs being carried out, or to be carried out, in the Atlantic region by other government departments and agencies. It will be used as a stopgap to fill needs which could not otherwise be provided for.
That is exactly what I said last night.
The special fund will not be used for financing projects which would be the normal or general responsibility of an existing department or agency. In every case, projects to be assisted or financed by the fund will require the approval of the governor in council. In this the working of the new board will be identical with the old.

I wonder if I could give the minister a moment to catch his breath, although I doubt that he needs it. I recall in the last parliament that he stated the Atlantic board was not going to report to the public, and also that it would be a lot closer to parliament if a minister of the crown were appointed chairman of the board. I wonder if it is the intention of the government that a minister should be chairman of the board and if so, will it be the Secretary of State?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think on reflection I came to the conclusion that it would be harder to get my legislation through the house if I made that suggestion. I was a little afraid that hon. gentlemen opposite might be a little inclined to suggest that if such a recommendation was made the board would not have that non-partisan character which I am very anxious it should have and, what is more important, that it would not appear to have the non-partisan character I want it to appear to have as well as to have.
What about the Minister of Agriculture?
Carried.
May I call it ten o'clock?
No.
Very well. I have only a few remarks.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Pictou is the only other speaker, I wonder if
18, 1963	1313
Business of the House hon. members would agree to hear him so that we could see the bill. We cannot come back to this for at least a week and I think it would be a great help to have the bill available for study in the Atlantic provinces and elsewhere.

If I
might say a word on that, we on this side have various speakers who want to contribute to this debate. Before I sit down I want to say, in connection with the observations of the Secretary of State about Sunday school that when a man implies to this house that the previous government did so little in six years, then we submit we need a chance to present the facts to this house and the country.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could not the hon. gentleman do that just as well on the bill as on the resolution, and not hold up the resolution just for that? The hon. gentleman would have unlimited time on the bill, not just half an hour.
We have two speakers at least who want to contribute to this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It being ten o'clock shall I rise, report progress, and request leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, everyone is aware that the budget debate commences tomorrow and lasts for six sitting days without interruption unless some unforeseen emergency occurs. I was wondering if the house leader, the Secretary of State, would just like to record the fact in Hansard for the benefit of hon. members who may not be here tonight?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has stated the position correctly.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, June 19, 1963
